points.title: A or an?
points.summary: Use **a** before a consonant **sound** (*a car, a university*) and **an** before a vowel **sound** (*an apple, an hour*). Only with singular countable nouns.

points.title: A or the? First mention and things we both know
points.summary: Use **a / an** the first time you mention something. Use **the** when it's clear which one: *I saw a cat. The cat was black.* Also **the** for things there's only one of: *the sun, the moon*.

points.title: A / an for jobs, descriptions, prices and frequency
points.summary: Use **a / an** for jobs (*She's a nurse*), descriptions (*It's a beautiful day*), **what a…!** and to mean **per** (*twice a week, $5 a kilo*).

points.title: The cinema, the piano, the same, the best
points.summary: Use **the** with common places in town (*the bank, the cinema*), instruments (*play the guitar*), superlatives (*the best*), *the same, the first, the only*.

points.title: General statements: the tiger, a doctor, tigers; the rich
points.summary: To talk about a type in general: **plural** with no article (*Tigers are…*), **the + singular** (formal: *The tiger is…*), or **a + singular** (*A tiger can…*). **the + adjective** = a group of people (*the rich, the elderly*).

points.title: Advanced article use: a coffee, a good knowledge, the French, a Mr Smith
points.summary: Articles can change uncountable nouns into countable ones (*a coffee, a knowledge of*), refer to nationalities (*the French*), and show you don't know someone (*a Mr Smith called*).

points.title: Adjectives before nouns and after be
points.summary: Adjectives go **before a noun** (*a small flat*) or **after** *be, look, feel, seem, sound, taste, get* (*The flat is small*). They **don't** take *-s* in the plural: *two small flats*.

points.title: Opinion, size, age, colour: a lovely big old house
points.summary: With more than one adjective, put **opinion** first, then **facts**, usually in this order: **size → age → shape → colour → origin → material → purpose** + noun: *a lovely small old round wooden table* (but two or three adjectives are more natural).

points.title: And between adjectives: big and bright, black and white
points.summary: After a verb, join two adjectives with ***and***: *The room was big **and** bright.* With three, use commas and *and*: *clever, kind **and** funny*. Use ***and*** between colours of one thing: *a black **and** white photo*.

points.title: Adjectives after nouns: something new, the people involved
points.summary: Some adjectives go **after** the noun: after ***something, anyone, nowhere*** (*something interesting*), with some participles and *available* (*the people involved, the seats available*), and with measurements (*two metres long*).

points.title: Good at, afraid of, interested in
points.summary: Common pairs: **good / bad at**, **afraid / scared / proud / tired / full of**, **interested in**, **worried / excited about**, **keen on**, **famous for**.

points.title: Kind to, married to, similar to, good for
points.summary: **kind / nice / rude / polite to** someone; **angry / annoyed with** someone **about** something; **similar to**, **different from**, **married to**, **responsible for**, **aware of**, **capable of**, **good / bad for**.

points.title: Adjective + preposition + -ing
points.summary: After a preposition, use a **noun** or the **-ing** form, never the base verb: *I'm good at **cooking**. She's tired of **waiting**. Are you interested in **joining**?*

points.title: Good at, good with, good for; sorry about, sorry for
points.summary: Some adjectives take **different prepositions** with **different meanings**: *good at* (skill), *good with* (handling), *good for* (healthy), *kind of you* (an action); *sorry about* (a situation), *feel sorry for* (pity).

points.title: Prone to, devoid of, consistent with: formal pairs
points.summary: Formal and academic pairs: **prone / susceptible / conducive / averse to**, **devoid / indicative / wary of**, **consistent / compatible / synonymous with**, **reliant / contingent on**, **exempt from**, **adept at**.

points.title: This, such, the former and the latter
points.summary: Refer back to earlier ideas with ***this / that / these*** (+ noun), ***such*** (+ noun), ***the former*** (the first of two) and ***the latter*** (the second of two), so you don't repeat words.

points.title: Anyway, by the way, actually, mind you
points.summary: Spoken **discourse markers** help you manage a conversation: ***anyway*** (back to the main topic / ending), ***by the way*** (a new topic), ***actually*** (a correction or surprise), ***mind you*** (BrE: adding a contrast), ***I mean*** (explaining), ***as I was saying*** (returning to a topic).

points.title: In other words, namely, to sum up, that is to say
points.summary: Signposting in writing: **order** (*firstly, to begin with, lastly*), **rephrasing** (*in other words, that is to say, i.e.*), **examples** (*for instance, e.g., namely*), **summing up** (*to sum up, in conclusion, overall*).

points.title: Hence, thus, consequently, accordingly
points.summary: Formal **result** linkers: ***consequently***, ***as a consequence***, ***thus***, ***hence***, ***accordingly***. ***Hence*** can be followed by just a **noun**: *He's from Rome, **hence** his name, Romano.*

points.title: That said, admittedly, let alone, if anything
points.summary: Very advanced markers: **concession** (*admittedly, granted, that said, be that as it may, all the same*), **emphasis** (*indeed, if anything, not to mention, let alone*).

points.title: Always, usually, often, sometimes, never
points.summary: From most to least often: ***always*** (100%) > ***usually*** > ***often*** > ***sometimes*** > ***rarely / hardly ever*** > ***never*** (0%).

points.title: Word order: I always go, I'm always tired
points.summary: Adverbs of frequency go **before the main verb** (*I often go*) but **after** *be* (*I'm often late*) and **after** the first **auxiliary** (*I have never been, I can't always come*).

points.title: How often? Once a week, every day, twice a month
points.summary: Ask ***How often…?*** and answer with **expressions of frequency**: *every day, once a week, twice a month, three times a year, every other day*. These usually go at the **end** of the sentence.

points.title: Seldom, rarely, frequently, invariably; Rarely have I…
points.summary: More formal adverbs: ***frequently*** (often), ***occasionally*** (sometimes), ***seldom / rarely*** (not often), ***invariably*** (always, without exception). ***Rarely, seldom*** and ***never*** at the start of a sentence need **inversion**: *Rarely do we see such talent.*

points.title: Adjective or adverb? Quick or quickly?
points.summary: Use an **adjective** with a noun (*a quick lunch*) and an **adverb** with a verb (*She ate quickly*). Most adverbs = adjective + **-ly**.

points.title: Good or well? Hard, fast, late, early
points.summary: The adverb of ***good*** is ***well***. Some adverbs are the **same** as the adjective: ***hard, fast, late, early, straight***. ***Hardly*** and ***lately*** have different meanings.

points.title: Friendly, lively, lovely; look good, feel tired
points.summary: Some words ending in ***-ly*** are **adjectives**: *friendly, lovely, lonely, lively, silly, ugly*. For an adverb meaning, use ***in a … way***: *in a friendly way*. After **linking verbs** (*be, look, feel, sound, taste, smell, seem*), use an **adjective**: *You look tired.*

points.title: Hard or hardly? Free or freely? Wide or widely?
points.summary: Some pairs have **different meanings**: ***hard*** (with effort) / ***hardly*** (almost not); ***free*** (without paying) / ***freely*** (without limits); ***wide*** (fully) / ***widely*** (in many places); ***high*** / ***highly*** (very much); ***deep*** / ***deeply*** (very); ***near*** / ***nearly*** (almost).

although-despite-in-spite-of.h1: Although, Despite and In Spite Of

points.title: Although and though + clause
points.summary: ***Although*** (or ***though***) + subject + verb shows a surprising contrast: ***Although** it was cold, we went swimming.* Don't use *although* and *but* together.

points.title: Despite / in spite of + noun or -ing
points.summary: ***Despite*** and ***in spite of*** mean the same as *although*, but they're followed by a **noun**, a **pronoun** or ***-ing***: ***Despite** the rain… **In spite of** being tired…* Use ***despite the fact that*** + clause.

points.title: Even though, even if, and though at the end
points.summary: ***Even though*** = a stronger *although* (a real fact). ***Even if*** = it doesn't matter whether it happens (a possible situation). ***Though*** can also go at the **end** of a sentence, meaning *however*.

points.title: Whereas, while, on the other hand
points.summary: To compare **two different facts**, use ***whereas*** or ***while*** (*I like tea, **whereas** my wife likes coffee*) or ***On the other hand*** at the start of a new sentence. ***On the contrary*** is different: it means *that's not true; the opposite is true*.

points.title: Albeit, much as, notwithstanding, tired as I was
points.summary: Formal concession: ***albeit*** + adjective / adverb / noun phrase, ***much as*** + clause (= although I really), ***notwithstanding*** (= despite), ***adjective / adverb + as / though*** + clause (*Tired **as** I was, …*), ***however*** + adjective (*However hard I try, …*).

and-but-or-so-because.h1: And, But, Or, So and Because

points.title: And, but, or
points.summary: ***And*** adds information. ***But*** shows a **contrast** (a different or surprising idea). ***Or*** gives a **choice**.

points.title: So or because? Result and reason
points.summary: ***Because*** gives the **reason** (why?). ***So*** gives the **result** (what happened next?): *I was hungry, **so** I ate a sandwich. I ate a sandwich **because** I was hungry.*

points.title: Because or because of? So, that's why
points.summary: ***Because*** + a **clause** (subject + verb): *because **it was** raining*. ***Because of*** + a **noun**: *because of **the rain***. ***That's why*** = so (in speaking).

points.title: Also, too, as well, either
points.summary: ***Also*** goes **before** the main verb (after *be*): *I **also** play tennis.* ***Too*** and ***as well*** go at the **end**: *I play tennis **too / as well**.* In negatives, use ***either***: *I don't like it **either**.*

points.title: However, therefore, in addition, as a result
points.summary: In more formal writing, use linkers between sentences: ***However*** (contrast), ***Therefore / As a result*** (result), ***In addition / Moreover*** (adding). They usually start a new sentence, followed by a **comma**.

points.title: I'm going to…: plans and intentions
points.summary: **am / is / are going to + base verb** for things you've already decided to do: *I'm going to buy a new phone.*

points.title: Not going to and Are you going to…?
points.summary: Negative: **'m not / isn't / aren't going to**. Question: **Are you going to…? What are you going to do?**

points.title: Predictions from evidence: It's going to rain
points.summary: Use **be going to** for a prediction based on something we can see or know **now**: *Look at those clouds. It's going to rain.*

points.title: Going to or present continuous for plans?
points.summary: **be going to** = an intention (I've decided). **present continuous** = an arrangement (it's fixed with other people, a time and a place).

points.title: Was going to: plans that changed
points.summary: **was / were going to + base verb** = a past plan, often one that **didn't happen**: *I was going to call you, but I forgot.*

points.title: Going to: imminent events, if + going to, and in formal English
points.summary: **be going to** can show something is about to happen (*I'm going to sneeze*), and **if + going to** means *if you intend to* (*If you're going to drive, don't drink*).

be-to-be-about-to.h1: Be About To, Be Due To and Be To

points.title: Be about to: very soon
points.summary: **be about to + base verb** = something will happen very soon: *Hurry up! The film is about to start.* **was about to** = I was just going to.

points.title: Be due to: scheduled events
points.summary: **be due to + verb** = it's planned or expected at a particular time: *The train is due to arrive at 6.15.* **be due** + time: *The baby is due in May.*

points.title: On the point of, on the verge of, be set to
points.summary: **be on the point / verge of + -ing** = very close to doing something. **be set to + verb** (news) = expected to happen soon: *Prices are set to rise.*

points.title: Be to: official plans and orders
points.summary: **be to + base verb** for official arrangements (*The President is to visit Japan*) and for orders (*You are to stay here*). **If … is to** = if … wants to / is going to.

points.title: Was to and was to have done: destiny and plans that failed
points.summary: **was to + verb** = something that happened later, seen from the past (*He was to become president*). **was to have + past participle** = a plan that didn't happen.

because-as-since.h1: Because, As, Since and Due To

points.title: Because, as and since
points.summary: ***Because***, ***as*** and ***since*** all give a reason + clause. ***Because*** puts more focus on the reason and is the usual answer to *Why?* ***As*** and ***since*** often start the sentence when the reason is clear or already known.

points.title: Now that, seeing as, in case
points.summary: ***Now that*** = because of a **new** situation (*Now that I've retired, I have more time*). ***Seeing as / seeing that*** (informal) = because. Don't confuse reasons with ***in case*** (a precaution: *Take an umbrella **in case** it rains*).

points.title: Due to, owing to, thanks to, because of
points.summary: ***Because of, due to, owing to*** and ***thanks to*** + **noun** or ***-ing***. ***Due to*** often follows *be* (*The delay **was due to** the snow*). ***Thanks to*** is usually for **good** results. Use ***due to the fact that*** + clause.

points.title: Given that, in that, inasmuch as, for, in view of
points.summary: Formal ways to give reasons: ***given (that)***, ***in view of***, ***on account of***, ***in that*** (= because, explaining in what way), ***inasmuch as***, and literary ***for*** (= because, after the main clause).

both-either-neither-not-only.h1: Both… And, Either… Or, Neither… Nor, Not Only… But Also

points.title: Both… and
points.summary: ***Both X and Y*** = X and Y, the two together: *Both my mother and my father are teachers.* With two subjects, use a **plural** verb.

points.title: Either… or: one or the other
points.summary: ***Either X or Y*** = X or Y, one of the two: *We can either take the bus or walk.* In negatives, ***not… either… or*** = not X and not Y. With two subjects, the verb agrees with the **nearest** one.

points.title: Neither… nor: not one and not the other
points.summary: ***Neither X nor Y*** = not X and not Y: *Neither my brother nor my sister can swim.* Use a **positive** verb, because *neither… nor* is already negative.

points.title: Not only… but also
points.summary: ***Not only X but (also) Y*** = X and also Y, with emphasis on the **second** idea: *She's not only clever but also very kind.* At the **start** of a sentence, use **inversion**: *Not only did he forget my birthday, but he also…*

points.title: Parallel structure, nor after a negative, whether… or
points.summary: Paired conjunctions join **parallel** items (the same grammar): *either **to stay** or **to leave***. ***Nor*** can start a new clause after a negative, with **inversion**: *He didn't call, **nor did he** write.* ***Whether… or*** = it doesn't matter which.

can-could-be-able-to.h1: Can, Could and Be Able To (Ability and Possibility)

points.title: Can and can't: ability
points.summary: **can / can't + base verb** for ability: *I **can** swim. She **can't** drive. **Can** you cook?*

points.title: Could and couldn't: ability in the past
points.summary: **could / couldn't + base verb** for general ability in the past: *I **could** swim when I was five. I **couldn't** sleep last night.*

points.title: Be able to: other tenses and after other verbs
points.summary: Use **be able to** where *can* is impossible: *I'll **be able to** help tomorrow. I've never **been able to** dance. I'd like to **be able to** ski.*

points.title: Could or was able to? Managed to
points.summary: For **one successful action** in the past, use **was able to** or **managed to**, not *could*: *The fire spread, but everyone **was able to** escape.*

points.title: Could and can for possibility and suggestions
points.summary: **could** = something is possible (*It could rain later*) or a suggestion (*We could go to the cinema*). **can** = something is generally possible (*You can see the sea from here*).

points.title: Can for typical behaviour, could for criticism
points.summary: **can** = what is typical, sometimes true: *She **can** be very rude.* **could** = criticism or irritation: *You **could** at least say thank you!*

points.title: Expressions with can and could
points.summary: Common fixed phrases: *I **couldn't agree** more. I **can't help** laughing. I **can't stand** it. I **could do with** a coffee. You **can't be** serious!*

causative-have-get.h1: Causative Have and Get (I had my hair cut)

points.title: Have something done: services
points.summary: **have + object + past participle** = arrange for someone to do it: *I have my hair cut every month. We had the house painted.*

points.title: Get something done
points.summary: **get + object + past participle** means the same as *have something done*, but it's more informal: *I need to get my phone fixed.* It can also mean *finish*: *get the work done*.

points.title: Had my phone stolen: things that happen to you
points.summary: **have / get + object + past participle** also describes bad things that **happen** to you, not things you arrange: *I had my bag stolen. He got his nose broken.*

points.title: Have someone do, get someone to do, make and let
points.summary: **have + person + base verb** and **get + person + to + verb** = arrange for someone to do something: *I'll have the porter carry your bags. I got my brother to help me.*

points.title: Have someone doing, I won't have it, get things going
points.summary: **have + person + -ing** = cause an ongoing result (*He had us laughing*). **won't have + person + -ing** = won't allow (*I won't have you talking like that*). **get + object + -ing** = start something (*get the car going*).

points.title: Emphatic do: I do like it! Do sit down.
points.summary: Put ***do / does / did*** before the base verb in a **positive** sentence to add **emphasis** or **contrast**: *I **do** like your dress! She **did** call you. I don't eat meat, but I **do** eat fish.* ***Do*** + imperative is polite and warm: ***Do** come in!*

points.title: It was Ali who…: it-clefts
points.summary: ***It is / It was*** + the focused part + ***who / that*** + the rest: ***It was Ali who** broke the window* (not someone else). ***It's the price that** worries me* (not the size).

points.title: What I need is a holiday: what-clefts
points.summary: ***What*** + clause + ***is / was*** + the focused part: ***What I need is** a holiday. **What I like about her is** her honesty.* The focus comes **at the end**.

points.title: All I want is, the thing is, the reason why
points.summary: Other cleft patterns: ***All I want is…*** (= the only thing), ***The thing (that) I…is***, ***The reason (why)…is that***, ***The place where…***, ***The person who…***, ***The first / last / only thing…***.

points.title: What she did was call the police; what happened was
points.summary: To focus on an **action**, use ***What*** + subject + ***do / did*** + ***is / was*** + (*to*) + base verb: ***What she did was (to) call** the police.* To focus on a whole event: ***What happened was (that)…***

points.title: It wasn't until, it's not that…it's that, that's what
points.summary: Advanced patterns: ***It wasn't until*** + time + ***that*** (= only then), ***It's not that … , it's (just) that…***, and **reversed** clefts: ***That's what** I mean. **This is where** the problem starts. **Here's why**…*

points.title: Bigger, more expensive, the biggest, the most expensive
points.summary: Short adjectives take **-er / the -est** (*cheap → cheaper → the cheapest*). Long adjectives take **more / the most** (*expensive → more expensive → the most expensive*). Use **than** after a comparative.

points.title: Good, better, best; bad, worse, worst; far, further
points.summary: Irregular forms: **good → better → the best**, **bad → worse → the worst**, **far → farther / further → the farthest / the furthest**. The adverbs **well** and **badly** also become **better** and **worse**.

points.title: As… as, not as… as, the same as
points.summary: Use ***as + adjective + as*** to say two things are **equal**: *She's as tall as her mother.* ***Not as / not so… as*** = less: *Ottawa isn't as big as Toronto.* Use ***the same as*** for things that are equal.

points.title: Much bigger, a bit cheaper, by far the best
points.summary: Make comparatives stronger with ***much, a lot, far*** (*much bigger*) and weaker with ***a bit, a little, slightly*** (*a bit cheaper*). Make superlatives stronger with ***by far*** (*by far the best*).

points.title: The more, the better; colder and colder
points.summary: ***The + comparative…, the + comparative*** shows two things changing together: *The more you practise, the better you get.* ***Comparative + and + comparative*** shows a continuing change: *It's getting colder and colder.*

points.title: Superior to, nowhere near as, twice the size of, the latter
points.summary: Formal and advanced comparison: ***superior / inferior / preferable to*** (not *than*), ***nowhere near as / not nearly as*** (much less), ***twice the size of***, ***the former / the latter***, and ***more + adjective + than + adjective*** for two qualities.

conditionals-unless-provided.h1: Unless, As Long As, Provided, In Case and Even If

points.title: Unless = if … not
points.summary: **unless** = *if … not*. Use a **positive** verb after it: *I'll go **unless** it rains* (= if it doesn't rain).

points.title: As long as, provided (that), providing
points.summary: **as long as / provided (that) / providing** = only if: *You can borrow my car **as long as** you're careful.*

points.title: In case: a precaution
points.summary: **in case** = because something **might** happen: *Take an umbrella **in case** it rains.* It's different from *if*.

points.title: Even if, even though and whether or not
points.summary: **even if** = it doesn't matter if: *I'll go **even if** it rains.* **even though** = although (a fact). **whether or not** = in both cases.

points.title: When unless doesn't work, and only if
points.summary: *Unless* = *except if*. Don't use it for feelings or results of *not* happening (*I'd be upset if you didn't come*). **Only if** makes the condition the one and only condition.

points.title: Countable or uncountable?
points.summary: **Countable** nouns have a singular and a plural (*an apple, two apples*). **Uncountable** nouns have no plural and no *a / an* (*water, rice, money*), and they take a singular verb.

points.title: Tricky uncountable nouns: advice, information, news
points.summary: Some nouns are **uncountable** in English but countable in many other languages: *advice, information, news, furniture, luggage, homework, equipment, traffic, weather, work, travel*.

points.title: A piece of, a slice of, a bottle of
points.summary: To count uncountable nouns, use a **unit**: *a piece of cake, a slice of bread, a bottle of water, a cup of coffee, a bar of chocolate, a loaf of bread*.

points.title: Nouns that can be both: paper or a paper, coffee or a coffee
points.summary: Many nouns can be **countable or uncountable** with a different meaning: *paper* (material) / *a paper* (a newspaper); *glass* / *a glass*; *time* / *a time*; *experience* / *an experience*. With drinks, *a coffee* = a cup of coffee.

points.title: Formal uncountable nouns: research, evidence, feedback
points.summary: In formal and academic English, *research, evidence, feedback, knowledge, progress, accommodation, equipment* are **uncountable**. Use *a piece of*, *a study* or another countable word for one. Some uncountable nouns become countable for **kinds** (*French wines*).

defining-relative-clauses.h1: Defining Relative Clauses (the man who…, the book that…)

points.title: Who, which and that
points.summary: **who** for people, **which** for things, **that** for both: *the girl who / that won*, *the car which / that I bought*.

points.title: Leaving out who, which or that: the people we met
points.summary: When the relative pronoun is the **object** of the clause, you can leave it out: *the book (that) I'm reading, the people (who) we met*.

points.title: Whose, where and when
points.summary: **whose** = of whom / of which (*the man whose car was stolen*). **where** = in / at which (*the town where I grew up*). **when** = time (*the day when we met*).

points.title: Prepositions in relative clauses: the house I live in
points.summary: In everyday English, the preposition goes at the **end**: *the house I live in, the person I spoke to*. In formal English: *the person to whom I spoke*.

points.title: Who or whom?
points.summary: **whom** is the formal object form of *who*: *the man whom I met*. In everyday English, people use **who** or **that**, or leave it out. After a preposition, always **whom**.

points.title: What or that? Everything that, all that, what you need
points.summary: **what** = *the thing(s) that*. Don't use *what* after a noun or after *everything, all, something, nothing*: use **that**: *Everything that he said was true.*

points.title: Reduced relative clauses: the woman talking to Tom, a car made in Japan
points.summary: Shorten relative clauses with **-ing** (active: *the man sitting there* = who is sitting) or a **past participle** (passive: *the car stolen yesterday* = which was stolen).

points.title: The first to arrive, nothing to do, the reason why, the way
points.summary: Infinitive relative clauses: **the first / last / only / next + to + verb** (*the first person to arrive*), **something / nothing + to + verb** (*nothing to do*). Also **the reason (why / that)** and **the way (that / in which)**.

points.title: Bored or boring? Interested or interesting?
points.summary: ***-ed*** = how you **feel** (*I'm tired*). ***-ing*** = what **causes** the feeling (*My job is tiring*).

points.title: Confused or confusing? Embarrassed or embarrassing?
points.summary: Other common pairs: *confused / confusing, embarrassed / embarrassing, disappointed / disappointing, frightened / frightening, worried / worrying, annoyed / annoying, relaxed / relaxing, shocked / shocking*.

points.title: Overwhelmed, intrigued, unsettling: advanced pairs
points.summary: Advanced pairs follow the same rule: *overwhelmed / overwhelming, intrigued / intriguing, exhausted / exhausting, fascinated / fascinating, horrified / horrifying, unsettled / unsettling, inspired / inspiring, humiliated / humiliating*.

points.title: One and ones: the red one, these ones
points.summary: Use ***one*** (singular) and ***ones*** (plural) instead of repeating a **countable noun**: *I don't like this jacket. I prefer the black **one**. These shoes are nicer than the old **ones**.*

points.title: I'd love to, I didn't want to: to instead of the whole verb
points.summary: Use ***to*** alone instead of repeating the **whole infinitive**: *Would you like to come? ~ I'd love **to**. I didn't want to go, but I had **to**.*

points.title: She went out and bought milk: leaving out repeated words
points.summary: After ***and, but, or***, we often leave out a **repeated subject**, **auxiliary** or **verb**: *She went out and (she) bought some milk. I can sing but (I) can't dance. Ali ordered fish and Sara (ordered) chicken.*

points.title: Do so, do that, if so, if not, I'm afraid so
points.summary: Substitute a whole verb phrase with ***do so*** (formal), ***do that / do it*** (informal). Replace a whole clause with ***so*** (*If so…, I'm afraid so*) or ***not*** (*If not…, I hope not*).

points.title: Want a coffee? Sounds good. Seen Ali?
points.summary: In **informal speech**, we often leave out words at the **start** of a sentence (subjects and auxiliaries) when the meaning is clear: *(Do you) **Want** a coffee? (It) **Sounds** good. (Have you) **Seen** Ali? (I'm) **Sorry** I'm late.*

points.title: As did we, than do most people, so would I
points.summary: Formal **comparative and additive** patterns use an auxiliary (often with **inversion**): *She was tired, **as were** we. They earn more **than do** most people. He loved the film, **as did** I.*

points.title: For + a period, since + a starting point
points.summary: **for** + a length of time (*for three hours, for ten years*); **since** + the time it started (*since 9 am, since Monday, since 2019*).

points.title: Ago, for or since?
points.summary: **ago** = how long before now something happened (past simple): *I came two years ago.* **for / since** = how long a situation has continued (present perfect).

points.title: How long have you…? or When did you…?
points.summary: *How long **have** you **been** here?* (up to now) vs *When **did** you **arrive**?* (a point in the past). Don't use the present simple for *how long* up to now.

points.title: It's two years since… and I haven't… for…
points.summary: Three ways to say the same thing: *It's two years since I saw her. I haven't seen her for two years. The last time I saw her was two years ago.*

points.title: Since + a clause, ever since, and since meaning because
points.summary: **since** + past simple clause for the starting point: *since I left school*. **ever since** = all the time from then until now. **since** can also mean *because*.

points.title: Over the last few years, in years, during, throughout
points.summary: **over / in the last** + period with the present perfect for a period up to now; **in years / for ages** after negatives; **during / throughout** for a period.

fronting-for-emphasis.h1: Fronting and Word Order for Emphasis

points.title: On the hill stood a castle; off they went
points.summary: After a fronted **place or direction** phrase, verbs like *stand, lie, sit, come, go, run, live* can come **before a noun subject**: ***On the hill stood** an old castle. **Down came** the rain.* With a **pronoun** subject, there's no inversion: ***Off they went.***

points.title: This I can't accept: fronting objects and complements
points.summary: Put an **object** or **complement** first for **contrast** or emphasis, with **normal word order** after it: ***This** I can't accept. **The first film** I loved; **the second** I hated. **Strange people** they were.*

points.title: Gone are the days, attached is my CV
points.summary: Fronted **participles** and **adjectives** + ***be*** + subject: ***Gone are** the days when… **Attached is** my CV. **Included** in the price **are** breakfast and dinner. **Lucky are** those who…*

points.title: More important is, equally worrying was, such is
points.summary: Fronted **comparatives** and **evaluating adjectives** + ***be*** + subject: ***More important** than money **is** health. **Equally worrying was** the lack of staff. **Even more surprising** **is** the price.* Also ***Such is*** + noun + ***that***.

points.title: Try as I might, come what may, suffice it to say
points.summary: Fixed fronted patterns: ***Try as I might*** (= although I tried hard), ***Come what may*** (= whatever happens), ***Be it … or …*** (= whether it's), ***Suffice it to say*** (= I'll just say), ***So be it*** (= I accept it), ***Far be it from me to…***.

future-continuous-future-perfect.h1: Future Continuous and Future Perfect (will be doing, will have done)

points.title: Future continuous: will be doing
points.summary: **will be + -ing** for an action in progress at a particular time in the future: *At 8 tonight I'll be watching the match.*

points.title: Will you be using…? Polite questions and things that will happen anyway
points.summary: **Will you be + -ing?** asks politely about someone's plans: *Will you be using the car tonight?* It also describes things that will happen as a matter of course: *I'll be seeing Ali tomorrow.*

points.title: Future perfect: will have done by…
points.summary: **will have + past participle** for something that will be **complete** before a time in the future: *By 2030 I'll have paid off my loan.*

points.title: Future perfect continuous: will have been doing
points.summary: **will have been + -ing** for the duration of an activity up to a point in the future: *By June, I'll have been working here for ten years.*

future-in-the-past.h1: Future in the Past (was going to, would…)

points.title: The future seen from the past: four forms
points.summary: **would** (from *will*), **was going to** (from *going to*), **was + -ing** (from present continuous), **was about to** (from *be about to*).

points.title: Would as the future in the past (reported speech and thoughts)
points.summary: After past reporting and thinking verbs (*said, thought, knew, hoped*), **will** becomes **would**: *She said she would come. I thought it would rain.*

points.title: Little did she know she would…: hints about the future in stories
points.summary: In stories, **would** and **was to** look ahead from the past to what happened later: *It was a decision she **would** regret for the rest of her life.*

points.title: Plans that didn't happen: was going to, was hoping to, had intended to
points.summary: Several forms describe past plans that **didn't happen**: *was going to, was supposed to, was hoping to, had intended to, was to have done, would have liked to*.

future-time-clauses.h1: Future Time Clauses (When I get home, I'll…)

points.title: When, as soon as, before, after + present
points.summary: For the future, use **present simple** after *when, as soon as, before, after, until*: *I'll text you **as soon as** I **arrive**.*

points.title: When I've finished…: present perfect in time clauses
points.summary: Use the **present perfect** in a time clause to show that the first action will be **complete** before the second: *I'll call you when I've finished work.*

points.title: Until, once, by the time, the moment, next time
points.summary: Other time words follow the same rule: *I'll wait **until** you **arrive**. **Once** you **know** the rules, it's easy. **By the time** we **get** there, the film **will have started**.*

points.title: When will is correct after when and if
points.summary: *Will* is correct after *when* in **questions and noun clauses** (*I don't know when he'll come*), and after *if* for **willingness** (*if you'll wait*). Only time clauses take the present.

points.title: Like, love, hate + -ing
points.summary: After **like, love, hate, enjoy**, use **-ing**: *I like swimming. She loves reading. They hate getting up early.* (*Like / love / hate + to* is also correct.)

points.title: Want to, need to, decide to, hope to
points.summary: After **want, need, would like, decide, hope, plan, try, learn, forget, promise**, use **to + base verb**: *I want to travel. She decided to leave.*

points.title: Enjoy, finish, mind, stop, avoid + -ing
points.summary: After **enjoy, finish, mind, stop, avoid, keep, suggest, miss, practise**, use **-ing**: *Have you finished eating? I can't stop laughing.*

points.title: Want someone to do: verb + object + to
points.summary: **want / would like / ask / tell / expect / help + person + to + verb**: *I want you to come. She asked me to help her.* Not *I want that you come*.

points.title: After prepositions: -ing (interested in learning, before leaving)
points.summary: After a **preposition** (*in, at, of, for, about, before, after, without*), use **-ing**: *I'm interested in learning Chinese. Think before speaking.*

points.title: Common verbs + -ing and verbs + to
points.summary: Learn the most common patterns: **+ -ing**: *admit, avoid, consider, deny, imagine, keep, mind, miss, practise, risk, suggest*. **+ to**: *afford, agree, arrange, decide, expect, fail, hope, manage, offer, plan, promise, refuse, seem*.

points.title: -ing as a subject; it's worth -ing; it's no use -ing
points.summary: **-ing** can be the subject: *Swimming is good for you.* Useful phrases: **it's worth -ing, it's no use -ing, there's no point (in) -ing, have difficulty / trouble (in) -ing**.

points.title: See someone do or see someone doing?
points.summary: After **see, hear, watch, notice, feel**: **object + base verb** = the whole action (*I saw him cross the road*). **object + -ing** = part of an action in progress (*I saw him crossing the road*).

points.title: Perfect and passive forms: having done, to have done, being done
points.summary: **having + past participle** and **to have + past participle** show an earlier action: *He denied having stolen it. She seems to have left.* **being + past participle** and **to be + past participle** are passive.

points.title: Very cold, absolutely freezing
points.summary: Use ***very / extremely / a bit*** with **gradable** adjectives (*very big*). Use ***absolutely*** or ***really*** with **extreme** adjectives (*absolutely huge*). ***Really*** works with both.

points.title: Absolute adjectives: completely different, almost empty
points.summary: **Absolute** adjectives describe all-or-nothing qualities: *impossible, perfect, unique, dead, empty, full, finished, different, wrong, right*. Use ***completely, totally, absolutely, entirely*** with them, and ***almost / nearly*** for “not quite”: *almost empty*.

points.title: Highly unlikely, deeply concerned: adverb + adjective pairs
points.summary: Advanced English uses natural **adverb + adjective** pairs instead of *very*: ***highly** unlikely, **deeply** concerned, **bitterly** disappointed, **fully** aware, **perfectly** normal, **seriously** injured*.

points.title: I've got, she's got: forms
points.summary: ***I / you / we / they have got*** ('ve got). ***He / she / it has got*** ('s got). Use it for things you **own**, **family**, **appearance** and **illness**.

points.title: I haven't got, have you got…?
points.summary: **Negative**: ***haven't got / hasn't got***. **Questions**: ***Have you got…? Has she got…?*** Short answers: *Yes, I have. No, she hasn't.* (not *Yes, I've got*)

points.title: Have got or have? Have breakfast, had a car
points.summary: ***Have got*** and ***have*** mean the same for **possession**. But use only ***have*** for **actions** (*have breakfast, have a shower, have a party*) and in the **past** (*I had a bike*, not *I had got a bike*).

points.title: Have got to, got and gotten
points.summary: ***Have got to*** + verb = ***have to*** (obligation, informal): *I**'ve got to** go.* In American English, the past participle of *get* is often ***gotten*** (*It's gotten cold*), but ***have got*** (possession) is the same in both.

points.title: May, might, could, tend to, seem to
points.summary: Soften claims with **modal verbs** (*may, might, could*), ***tend to*** (= usually), and ***seem / appear to***: *This **may** be the reason. Young people **tend to** spend more online. The plan **seems to** work.*

points.title: Probably, possibly, largely, to some extent
points.summary: **Adverbs** and phrases soften or limit a claim: ***probably, possibly, perhaps, apparently, arguably, generally, largely, relatively, to some extent, in some cases***.

points.title: It would appear that, it could be argued that
points.summary: Impersonal ***it*** patterns make claims more **careful** and **objective**: ***It would appear that…, It seems likely that…, It could be argued that…, There is some evidence that…, This suggests that…***

points.title: Is said to have, would seem to suggest, reportedly
points.summary: **Distancing** shows that a claim comes from **others**, not from you: ***is said / thought / believed to (have)…***, ***reportedly, allegedly, supposedly***, ***according to***. Combine hedges for very careful claims: ***would seem to suggest***.

points.title: Open the door. Don't run.
points.summary: **Positive**: base verb (*Sit down. Be quiet.*). **Negative**: ***Don't*** + base verb (*Don't worry. Don't be late.*). Use it for instructions, orders, advice and warnings.

points.title: Let's go, let's not, shall we?
points.summary: ***Let's*** + base verb makes a **suggestion** that includes **you and me**: ***Let's** go to the beach.* Negative: ***Let's not*** + verb (*Let's not argue*). Add ***shall we?*** to make it softer.

points.title: Please, make sure, don't forget to
points.summary: Make imperatives friendlier with ***please***, ***just***, and phrases like ***Make sure you…***, ***Don't forget to…***, ***Remember to…***, ***Feel free to…***, ***Have a…***

points.title: You sit here. Somebody call a doctor!
points.summary: Sometimes imperatives have a **subject** for **emphasis** or **contrast**: ***You** sit here, and **I'll** sit there.* With ***someone / everybody***: ***Somebody** call an ambulance! **Everyone** listen.* And ***Don't you dare…!*** (a strong warning).

points.title: Study hard and you'll pass; hurry up, or we'll be late
points.summary: **Imperative + *and*** = *if you do this, the result will happen*: ***Study** hard **and** you'll pass.* **Imperative + *or / or else*** = *if you don't, something bad will happen*: ***Hurry** up, **or** we'll miss the train.*

points.title: Do you know where…? I don't know what…
points.summary: After **Do you know…? / I don't know…**, use **statement order**: *Do you know where she **lives**?* (not *where does she live*)

points.title: If and whether: indirect yes/no questions
points.summary: For yes/no questions, use **if** or **whether**: *Is she coming?* → *Do you know **if / whether** she's coming?*

points.title: Could you tell me…? Polite indirect questions
points.summary: Indirect questions make requests for information more **polite**: *Could you tell me where the toilets are? Would you mind telling me how old you are?*

points.title: What to do, whether to go: question word + to-infinitive
points.summary: After verbs like **know, decide, wonder, ask, explain**, a question word + **to + verb** can replace a full clause: *I don't know what to say. She can't decide whether to go.*

points.title: What he said is true: question-word clauses as subjects and objects
points.summary: A clause like **what he said, where she lives, how it works** can act as a noun: as a **subject** (*What he said is true*) or an **object** (*I understand why you're upset*).

infinitive-of-purpose.h1: Infinitive of Purpose (to, for, so that, in order to)

points.title: To + verb: I went to the shop to buy bread
points.summary: Use **to + base verb** to say why: *I'm saving money to buy a car. She called to say sorry.*

points.title: To or for? For + noun, for + -ing
points.summary: **to + verb** for an action: *I went out to get some milk.* **for + noun**: *I went out for some milk.* **for + -ing** for what a thing is used for: *a knife for cutting bread.*

points.title: So that + can / could / will / would
points.summary: Use **so that** + subject + **can / could / will / would** for a purpose, especially when the subject changes: *I'll write it down so that I don't forget. She spoke slowly so that we could understand.*

points.title: In order to, so as to (and the negative)
points.summary: **in order to / so as to + verb** are more formal ways to give a purpose. For a negative purpose, use **in order not to / so as not to** (not *not to* alone).

points.title: With a view to, with the aim of, for fear of, lest
points.summary: Formal purpose expressions: **with a view to / with the aim of + -ing**, **for fear of + -ing / for fear that**, and very formal **lest** (= so that … not).

points.title: It's raining, it's 5 o'clock, it's 10 km
points.summary: Use ***it*** as the subject for **weather**, **time**, **dates**, **days** and **distance**: ***It**'s cold. **It**'s half past six. **It**'s Monday. **It**'s 3 km to the station.*

points.title: It is or there is?
points.summary: ***There is / are*** says that something **exists** or is in a place (first mention): ***There's** a problem.* ***It is*** describes or identifies something **already known**: ***It's** a big problem.*

points.title: It's easy to learn, it's nice to meet you
points.summary: ***It's*** + **adjective** + ***to*** + verb: ***It's easy to** use. **It's nice to** meet you.* Add ***for*** + person: ***It's hard for me to** understand.* Also ***It takes*** + time + ***to***: ***It takes** an hour **to** get there.*

points.title: It's a shame that, it seems that, it doesn't matter
points.summary: ***It*** + *be* + adjective / noun + ***that***-clause: ***It's a shame that** you can't come. **It's obvious that** he's lying.* With verbs: ***It seems / appears / turns out that…*** ***It doesn't matter whether / what…***

points.title: I find it hard to, I'd appreciate it if, make it clear
points.summary: ***It*** can also be a **preparatory object**: ***I find it hard to** believe. **I'd appreciate it if** you could help. **She made it clear that** she was unhappy. **I take it** you're not coming.*

points.title: It's no use, it's worth, it goes without saying
points.summary: Fixed patterns: ***It's no use / no good*** + *-ing*, ***It's worth*** + *-ing*, ***It goes without saying that…***, ***It remains to be seen whether…***, ***It stands to reason that…***, ***It's not for me to…***

points.title: Never have I…, rarely do we…, little did I know
points.summary: After ***never, rarely, seldom, little*** at the start, use **auxiliary + subject**: ***Never have I** felt so happy. **Rarely do we** see snow here. **Little did she know** what would happen.*

points.title: Not only … but also, not until, not once
points.summary: ***Not only*** + auxiliary + subject + ***but (also)***: ***Not only is** it cheap, **but** it's **also** fast.* ***Not until*** + time / clause, then inversion in the main clause: ***Not until** midnight **did** they arrive.* ***Not once*** + inversion.

points.title: Only when, only after, only then, only by
points.summary: ***Only*** + time / condition expression at the start, then **inversion** in the main clause: ***Only when** I got home **did I** realise… **Only after** the meeting **did** we know… **Only then did** she understand.*

points.title: Under no circumstances, on no account, in no way
points.summary: Strong negative phrases at the start take **inversion**: ***Under no circumstances should** you open this door. **On no account must** you tell her. **At no time did** he say that. **Nowhere have I** seen…*

points.title: Hardly had I, no sooner, not a word did he say
points.summary: Very formal patterns: ***Hardly / Scarcely had*** + subject … ***when***, ***No sooner had*** + subject … ***than***, ***Not a (single)*** + noun + inversion (*Not a word did he say*), and ***So / Such*** + inversion (*So strong was the wind that…*).

inverted-conditionals.h1: Inverted Conditionals (Had I known…, Should you need…)

points.title: Had I known…: inverted third conditional
points.summary: **Had + subject + past participle** = *If + subject + had + past participle*: ***Had I known**, I would have helped.*

points.title: Were I…, Were she to…: inverted second conditional
points.summary: **Were + subject + noun / adjective** or **Were + subject + to + verb** = *If … were (to)*: ***Were I** in your position… **Were she to** resign…*

points.title: Should you need…: formal first conditional
points.summary: **Should + subject + base verb** = *If … happens (by chance)*: ***Should you need** help, please call us.*

points.title: Negative inversion: Had I not…, Were it not for…
points.summary: In the negative, put **not** after the subject: ***Had I not** seen it… **Were it not for**… **Should you not** wish…* No contractions.

points.title: When to use inverted conditionals
points.summary: Inversion is **formal**: use it in business writing, reports, speeches and literature. In everyday speech, *if* sounds more natural.

points.title: Like (similar to) or as (a job or role)?
points.summary: ***Like*** + noun = **similar to** (but not really): *He swims **like** a fish.* ***As*** + noun = a **real job, role or use**: *She works **as** a nurse. I used my scarf **as** a blanket.*

points.title: As I said, as usual, do as I say
points.summary: ***As*** + clause = **in the same way** or **in agreement with**: *Do **as** I say. **As** I said, … **As** you know, …* Fixed phrases: ***as usual***, ***as expected***. In informal English, ***like*** + clause is common (*like I said*).

points.title: Look like, look happy, what's it like?
points.summary: ***Look / sound / feel / taste / smell*** + **adjective** (*You look **tired***), but ***look like*** + **noun** (*You look **like** your dad*). ***What's it like?*** asks for a description; ***What does it look like?*** asks about appearance.

points.title: Look as if, sound as though, feel like
points.summary: ***Look / sound / seem / feel*** + ***as if / as though / like*** + **clause** describes how something seems: *It looks **as if** it's going to rain. You sound **as though** you've got a cold.* ***Like*** + clause is informal.

points.title: Such as, unlike, alike, likewise, as is often the case
points.summary: ***Such as*** (and *like*) introduce **examples**. ***Unlike*** = different from. ***Alike*** = similar (after the noun or verb). ***Likewise*** = in the same way. Formal ***as*** clauses: ***as is often the case***, ***as was expected***, ***as can be seen***.

points.title: Make a cake, do your homework
points.summary: ***Make*** = create or produce (*make a cake, make tea, make a mess*). ***Do*** = activities, work and jobs (*do homework, do the dishes, do sport*), and general actions with *something, anything, nothing, what*.

points.title: Make a mistake, do me a favour
points.summary: Common **fixed** pairs. **make**: *a mistake, a decision, money, progress, an effort, friends, a plan, an appointment, an excuse, a complaint, a suggestion*. **do**: *a favour, business, your best, damage, good, harm, research, a course, an exam* (BrE).

points.title: It made me laugh; she made me wait
points.summary: ***Make*** + person + **base verb** = cause or force someone to do something: *The film **made me laugh**. My boss **made me work** late.* ***Make*** + person + **adjective**: *It **made me happy**.* Passive: *I **was made to wait**.*

points.title: Make sense, make do with, could do with
points.summary: Useful expressions: ***make sense*** (be logical), ***make sure*** (check), ***make up your mind*** (decide), ***make the most of*** (use well), ***make do with*** (manage with less), ***make it*** (arrive / succeed), ***could do with*** (want, need), ***do without*** (manage without), ***have (nothing) to do with***.

points.title: Might and might not: perhaps
points.summary: **might / might not + base verb** = perhaps (now or in the future): *I **might** go to the party. It **might not** rain.*

points.title: May or might?
points.summary: **may** and **might** both mean *perhaps*. *May* is a little more formal and can sound a little more certain. Use *might* for unreal situations.

points.title: Might be doing: now or in the future
points.summary: **might / may be + -ing** = perhaps something is happening now, or is planned: *Don't call now. She **might be sleeping**. I **might be working** late tonight.*

points.title: Might as well, may as well
points.summary: **might / may as well + base verb** = there's no better option, so let's do it: *The bus isn't coming. We **might as well** walk.*

points.title: He may be rich, but…: may and might for concession
points.summary: **may / might … but** = I accept this is true, but something else is more important: *He **may** be rich, **but** he isn't happy.*

points.title: You might want to…, may well, might have told me
points.summary: **might** for polite suggestions (*You **might want to** check that*) and annoyance (*You **might have** told me!*). **may / might well** = probably.

points.title: Past condition, present result
points.summary: **if + past perfect, would + base verb**: an imaginary past and its result **now**: *If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.*

points.title: Present condition, past result
points.summary: **if + past simple, would have + past participle**: a present (or general) situation that would have changed the past: *If I spoke French, I would have understood him.*

points.title: Mixed conditionals with continuous forms and modals
points.summary: Mixed conditionals can use **could, might** and **continuous** forms: *If I hadn't missed the flight, I'd be lying on a beach now.*

points.title: Choosing the right conditional
points.summary: Ask two questions: Is the condition real or imaginary? Is each part about the past, the present or the future? Then choose the forms.

points.title: Must and can't: I'm sure
points.summary: **must** = I'm sure it's true. **can't** = I'm sure it isn't true. *He's been working all day. He **must** be tired. That **can't** be Tom. He's in Paris.*

points.title: Might, may, could: it's possible
points.summary: **might / may / could** = it's possible (perhaps true). **couldn't** = I'm sure it isn't. *He might be at work. It could be a virus.*

points.title: Must be doing, might be doing, can't be doing
points.summary: For actions **in progress now**, use **must / might / can't + be + -ing**: *She isn't answering. She **must be driving**.*

points.title: Must have done, can't have done: sure about the past
points.summary: **must have + past participle** = I'm sure it happened. **can't / couldn't have + past participle** = I'm sure it didn't happen.

points.title: Might have done, could have done: possible in the past
points.summary: **might / may / could have + past participle** = perhaps it happened. **might not have** = perhaps it didn't. *She might have missed the bus.*

points.title: That'll be the postman: will and should for assumptions
points.summary: **will / won't** for confident assumptions (*That'll be Ali at the door*). **should** for what we expect (*He should be home by now*).

points.title: Bound to, likely to, may well: other ways to show probability
points.summary: **be bound to / be sure to** = certain. **be likely to** = probable. **be unlikely to** = not probable. **may well / could well** = quite possible.

much-many-a-few-a-little.h1: Much, Many, A Lot Of, A Few, A Little

points.title: Much, many, a lot of; how much, how many
points.summary: Use ***many*** + plural nouns and ***much*** + uncountable nouns, mostly in **questions and negatives**. Use ***a lot of / lots of*** with both, especially in **positive** sentences. Ask ***How many…?*** and ***How much…?***

points.title: A few and a little: some, but not a lot
points.summary: ***A few*** + plural nouns and ***a little*** + uncountable nouns mean **some, a small amount**: *I have a few friends here. Can I have a little sugar?*

points.title: Few or a few? Little or a little?
points.summary: ***A few / a little*** = **some** (positive). ***Few / little*** (without *a*) = **not many / not much** (negative): *I have a few friends* (I'm OK). *I have few friends* (I'm lonely).

points.title: Too much, too many, plenty of, a large number of
points.summary: ***Too much / too many*** = more than you want. ***Plenty of*** = more than enough. In formal English: ***a large number of*** + plural nouns, ***a great deal of / a large amount of*** + uncountable nouns.

points.title: Much in formal writing, many a, a great many
points.summary: In **formal** English, ***much*** and ***many*** are common in positive sentences: *Much has been written about this.* ***Many a*** + singular noun = many (literary). ***A good / great many*** = a very large number.

points.title: Have to: it's necessary
points.summary: **have to / has to + base verb** = it's necessary: *I **have to** work on Saturday. She **has to** wear a uniform.*

points.title: Must: strong obligation and strong advice
points.summary: **must + base verb** for strong obligation, often the speaker's own feeling, and for rules: *I **must** call my mum. You **must** wear a seat belt.*

points.title: Mustn't or don't have to?
points.summary: **mustn't** = it's not allowed / don't do it. **don't have to** = it's not necessary (you can if you want).

points.title: Must or have to?
points.summary: **must** often = the speaker thinks it's necessary. **have to** = a rule or situation makes it necessary. For the past and future, use **had to / will have to**.

points.title: Had to, will have to, have had to
points.summary: *Must* has no past or future form. Use **had to** for the past, **will have to** for the future, **have had to** for the present perfect.

points.title: Need to, don't need to, needn't
points.summary: **need to** = it's necessary. **don't need to / needn't** = it isn't necessary: *You **needn't** come. You **don't need to** come.*

points.title: Formal obligation: be required to, be obliged to, be to
points.summary: Formal ways to talk about obligation: **be required to, be obliged to, be compelled to**. Orders and rules: **be to** (*You are to report at 9*). Prohibition: **be not permitted / be prohibited from**.

narrative-tenses.h1: Narrative Tenses: Telling Stories in the Past

points.title: The four narrative tenses and their jobs
points.summary: Past simple = the main events; past continuous = the background; past perfect = earlier events; past perfect continuous = earlier activities.

points.title: Going back in time and coming back
points.summary: Use the past perfect to go back to an earlier time, then return to the past simple. Don't put the whole flashback in the past perfect.

points.title: Time linkers in stories
points.summary: Linkers show when things happened: *when, as soon as, after, before, by the time, until, while, during, eventually, in the end, at last*.

points.title: Choosing the right tense in a story
points.summary: For each verb, ask: is it the next event, the background, an earlier event, or an earlier activity? The answer gives you the tense.

points.title: Making stories lively: other tenses in narratives
points.summary: Good storytellers also use the present for drama (*So I walk in and…*), *would* for repeated actions, and *was about to / was going to* for plans that changed.

points.title: Decide → decision, important → importance
points.summary: Many **verbs** and **adjectives** have a related **noun**. Common endings: ***-tion / -sion*** (*decision*), ***-ment*** (*development*), ***-al*** (*arrival*), ***-ure*** (*failure*), ***-ance / -ence*** (*importance*), ***-ity*** (*ability*), ***-ness*** (*awareness*).

points.title: Because prices rose → because of the rise in prices
points.summary: In formal writing, a **clause** (subject + verb) often becomes a **noun phrase**: *Because prices **rose** sharply…* → *Because of **the sharp rise in prices**…* *When he **arrived**…* → ***On his arrival**…*

points.title: Make a decision, carry out research, reach an agreement
points.summary: Formal English often uses a **general verb + noun** instead of a single verb: *decide → **make a decision**, investigate → **carry out an investigation**, agree → **reach an agreement***. Learn the right **verb + noun** partners.

points.title: Dense noun phrases, and when to avoid them
points.summary: Academic writing uses **dense noun phrases** with pre-modifiers (*a three-year government study*) and *of*-phrases. But **too many** nouns make a text hard to read: *There was an increase in the level of unemployment* is weaker than *Unemployment rose*.

non-defining-relative-clauses.h1: Non-Defining Relative Clauses (My sister, who lives in Paris, …)

points.title: Extra information: commas, who and which
points.summary: Use **commas** and **who / which** (not *that*). The pronoun can't be left out: *Tom, who I met at school, is a pilot.*

points.title: Defining or non-defining? The commas change the meaning
points.summary: Without commas = **which one** (*My brother who lives in Rome* = I have more than one brother). With commas = **extra information** (*My brother, who lives in Rome,* = I have one brother).

points.title: Which for a whole idea: He was late, which annoyed me
points.summary: **which** can refer to the **whole previous clause**, not just a noun: *She passed all her exams, which was a big surprise.*

points.title: Whose, where and when in non-defining clauses
points.summary: **whose, where, when** also work in non-defining clauses: *My neighbour, whose dog barks all night, …* *Rome, where I studied, …* *In 2020, when we moved, …*

points.title: Most of whom, some of which, all of whom
points.summary: After **quantifiers** (*some, many, most, all, none, both, neither, a few*) + **of**, use **whom** (people) or **which** (things): *I have two brothers, both of whom live abroad.*

points.title: Formal patterns: in which, at which point, by which time
points.summary: In formal English, a preposition can come before **which / whom**: *the house, in which he was born*. Fixed phrases: **at which point, by which time, in which case**.

points.title: Noun + noun: a bus stop, a shoe shop
points.summary: Put a noun **before** another noun to describe it: *a bus stop, a tennis ball, a shoe shop*. The first noun is usually **singular**, and the **second** noun is the main one.

points.title: One word, two words or a hyphen?
points.summary: Compound nouns can be written as **one word** (*toothbrush, bedroom*), **two words** (*bus stop, credit card*) or with a **hyphen** (*mother-in-law, check-in*). There's no fixed rule, so check a dictionary.

points.title: A ten-minute walk, a five-star hotel
points.summary: Use **number + noun** with a **hyphen** before a noun to describe time, age, size or value: *a ten-minute walk, a five-star hotel, a three-year-old girl*. The noun is **singular**: *a two-hour film* (not *two-hours*).

points.title: A coffee cup or a cup of coffee?
points.summary: **Noun + noun** describes the **type or purpose** (*a coffee cup* = a cup for coffee). ***Of*** describes the **contents** (*a cup of coffee*). ***'s*** is for things that **belong to** a person or are **made for** a group of people (*Ali's cup, a children's book*).

points.title: Compound adjectives and long noun phrases
points.summary: **Compound adjectives** with hyphens are common before nouns: *a well-known writer, a long-term plan, a part-time job, a high-quality product*. News and formal English also use **long noun + noun phrases**: *a government housing policy*.

points.title: The reason for, a solution to, a problem with
points.summary: Common pairs: **reason for**, **cause of**, **solution / answer / key to**, **invitation to**, **increase / rise in**, **demand / need for**, **problem with**, **relationship with**, **difference between**, **interest in**, **damage to**, **effect on**.

points.title: On purpose, by mistake, in advance, on holiday
points.summary: Fixed **preposition + noun** phrases: **on purpose**, **by mistake / accident / chance**, **in advance**, **in a hurry**, **on holiday / business**, **for sale**, **on sale**, **in danger**, **at risk**, **out of order**, **out of date**, **in charge of**.

points.title: An increase in or of? Attitude to, advantage over
points.summary: ***Increase / rise / fall in*** + the thing that changes (*a rise **in** prices*), but ***of*** + the **amount** (*a rise **of** 5%*). Other pairs: **attitude to / towards**, **advantage of / over**, **respect for**, **connection between / with**, **in contrast to / with**.

points.title: Impact on, insight into, emphasis on: formal pairs
points.summary: Formal and academic pairs: **impact / emphasis / influence on**, **insight into**, **approach / contribution / commitment / access / threat / alternative / exposure to**, **implications for**, **preference for**; and phrases like **in the light of**, **with regard to**, **on behalf of**, **in terms of**.

object-pronouns.h1: Object Pronouns: Me, Him, Her, Us, Them

points.title: Me, you, him, her, it, us, them after a verb
points.summary: Use an **object pronoun** after a verb: *I love **her**. She called **me**. We saw **them**.*

points.title: Object pronouns after prepositions: with me, for them
points.summary: Use **object pronouns** after **prepositions**: *with me, for her, about him, to us, from them*.

points.title: Me too, it's me, my friend and I
points.summary: In short answers and after ***be***, use **object pronouns** in everyday English: *Me too! Who's there? ~ It's me.* In a subject with **two people**, use the **subject** form, and put yourself **last**: *My friend and I went to the cinema.*

points.title: Than me or than I am? Between you and me
points.summary: After ***than*** and ***as***, use an **object pronoun** in everyday English (*She's taller than me*) or **subject + verb** in careful English (*She's taller than I am*). After prepositions like ***between*** and ***except***, always use the **object** form: *between you and me*.

points.title: -ing clauses: at the same time, or because
points.summary: An ***-ing*** clause can show an action **at the same time** (*Walking home, I met Ali*) or a **reason** (*Feeling ill, she stayed in bed*). The subject is the same as in the main clause.

points.title: Past participle clauses: built in 1900
points.summary: A **past participle** clause has a **passive** meaning: ***Built** in 1900, the house is now a museum.* (= The house was built in 1900.) ***Written** in simple English, the book is easy to read.*

points.title: The man sitting there, the car parked outside
points.summary: Participle clauses can replace **relative clauses**: *the man **sitting** there* (= who is sitting), *the car **parked** outside* (= which is parked), *people **living** in cities* (= who live).

points.title: Having finished, having been told
points.summary: ***Having*** + **past participle** shows that one action happened **before** another: ***Having finished** my work, I went home.* Passive: ***Having been told** the news, she called her mother.*

points.title: Dangling participles, and after / while / when + -ing
points.summary: The participle clause must have the **same subject** as the main clause. ***Walking** down the street, **the rain** started* is wrong (the rain wasn't walking). You can keep a conjunction: ***After leaving**, **while waiting**, **when using**, **once finished***.

points.title: With prices rising, the work done, weather permitting
points.summary: **Absolute** clauses have their **own subject**: ***The work done**, we went home.* ***With*** + noun + participle: ***With prices rising**, people spend less.* Fixed expressions: ***weather permitting***, ***all things considered***, ***generally speaking***.

passive-reporting-structures.h1: Passive Reporting Structures (It is said that…, He is believed to…)

points.title: It is said that…, It is believed that…
points.summary: **It + passive reporting verb + that** + clause: *It is said that he is very rich. It was reported that the minister had resigned.*

points.title: He is said to be…, She is believed to live…
points.summary: **subject + passive reporting verb + to-infinitive**: *He is said to be very rich. The suspect is believed to live in Spain.*

points.title: Is thought to have done, is believed to be doing
points.summary: Use **to have + past participle** for an earlier action (*He is believed to have left the country*) and **to be + -ing** for an action in progress (*She is thought to be working on a new book*).

points.title: There is said to be…, There are thought to be…
points.summary: With *there*, use **there + is / are + reporting verb + to be**: *There are said to be ghosts in the house.*

points.title: Be supposed to, allegedly, reportedly
points.summary: **be supposed to** = people say (*This café is supposed to be great*). In news: **allegedly, reportedly, apparently** and **according to** report information without claiming it's true.

passive-voice.h1: Passive Voice (It was made in China)

points.title: Present simple passive: is made, are sold
points.summary: **am / is / are + past participle**: *Cheese **is made** from milk. These phones **are made** in Korea.*

points.title: Past simple passive: was built, were invited
points.summary: **was / were + past participle**: *The castle **was built** in 1450. We **were invited** to the wedding.* Add **by** to say who did it.

points.title: When do we use the passive? And when do we need by?
points.summary: Use the passive when **who does it** is unknown, obvious or unimportant, or when we want to focus on the **action or result**. Use **by** only when the agent adds useful information.

points.title: Continuous and perfect passives: is being done, has been done
points.summary: Continuous: **is / was being + past participle**. Perfect: **has / had been + past participle**: *The road is being repaired. My bike has been stolen.*

points.title: Future and modal passives: will be done, can be done, must be done
points.summary: After **will, can, must, should, might**, use **be + past participle**: *The results will be announced tomorrow. This can't be done.*

points.title: Passive infinitives and -ing forms: to be done, being done
points.summary: After verbs that take **to**, use **to be + past participle**: *I want to be told.* After verbs that take **-ing**, use **being + past participle**: *I hate being interrupted.*

points.title: Get passive: get married, get paid, get hurt
points.summary: In informal English, **get + past participle** can replace *be* in the passive, often for changes, accidents or things we don't control: *He got injured. We get paid on Fridays.*

points.title: Passives with two objects: I was given…, She was offered…
points.summary: With verbs like **give, offer, send, show, tell, teach**, the person usually becomes the subject: *I was given a present.* (more natural than *A present was given to me*)

points.title: Complex passives: elected president, looked after, it was decided
points.summary: Passives with complements (*He was elected president*), prepositional verbs (*She was looked after*), and verbs that can't be passive (*happen, arrive, have*).

points.title: Form and use: in the middle of an action
points.summary: **was / were + -ing**: the action was in progress at a past moment. *At 8 I was having dinner.*

points.title: Negatives and questions
points.summary: Negative: **wasn't / weren't + -ing**. Question: **Was / Were + subject + -ing?**

points.title: Two actions in progress at the same time: while
points.summary: Two longer actions happening at the same time: *While I **was cooking**, he **was watching** TV.*

points.title: Setting the scene in a story
points.summary: Use the past continuous for the **background** of a story; use the past simple for the **events**.

points.title: Was always doing: annoying past habits
points.summary: **always / constantly + past continuous** for repeated past behaviour, often annoying: *He **was always losing** his keys.*

points.title: Temporary periods, repeated actions and duration
points.summary: The past continuous can show a temporary routine (*That summer I was working nights*) or stress duration (*I was cleaning all morning*).

points.title: I was wondering if…: polite requests and past plans
points.summary: *I **was wondering** if you could help* is a polite request about now. *She **was leaving** the next day* is a plan seen from the past.

points.title: Form and use: up to a moment in the past
points.summary: **had been + -ing** for an activity that continued up to (or until shortly before) a past moment, often with *for*, *since* or *how long*.

points.title: Explaining what we saw: She'd been crying
points.summary: Use the past perfect continuous to explain a past situation by an activity that happened just before it: *His eyes were red. He'd been crying.*

points.title: Had been doing or had done?
points.summary: **had been doing** = the activity and how long. **had done** = a completed action, a result, or how many. State verbs use **had done**.

points.title: Was doing or had been doing?
points.summary: **was doing** = in progress **at** that moment. **had been doing** = in progress **up to** that moment, often with how long.

points.title: Repeated activities and plans up to a past time
points.summary: The past perfect continuous can describe a **repeated** activity up to a past time (*She'd been phoning him all week*) and intentions: *I'd been meaning to call you.*

points.title: In reported speech
points.summary: In reported speech, the present perfect continuous and the past continuous often become the past perfect continuous: *I've been waiting* → *She said she had been waiting.*

points.title: Form and main use: something earlier in the past
points.summary: had + past participle for an action before another past moment.

points.title: Past simple or past perfect? The order of events
points.summary: Past simple for events in order; past perfect for an event that happened earlier than the one you're talking about.

points.title: By the time, already, just, never … before
points.summary: by the time + past simple, then past perfect; already, just, never … before with the past perfect.

points.title: Present perfect or past perfect?
points.summary: have done = before now; had done = before a moment in the past.

points.title: It was the first time I'd…; states up to a past moment
points.summary: It was the first time / the best … I'd ever + past perfect; state verbs up to a past moment use the past perfect simple.

points.title: When the past perfect is optional
points.summary: If the order is already clear (after, as soon as, before) the past simple is also fine; once the earlier time is set, you can continue in the past simple.

points.title: Past perfect in reported speech and thoughts
points.summary: A present perfect becomes past perfect when reported in the past; a past simple can become past perfect or stay the same.

points.title: Plans that didn't happen: I had hoped to…
points.summary: had hoped / meant / intended / planned / wanted to = a plan or wish that didn't happen.

points.title: A longer action and a short action
points.summary: Past continuous for the longer action in progress; past simple for the short action that happened in the middle of it.

points.title: When and while
points.summary: **While** usually goes before the longer action (past continuous). **When** usually goes before the shorter action (past simple).

points.title: How the tense changes the meaning
points.summary: *When I arrived, they **had** lunch* = after I arrived. *When I arrived, they **were having** lunch* = it was already in progress.

points.title: Finished or unfinished?
points.summary: The past simple often means the action was **completed**; the past continuous can mean it was **not completed**: *I read a book* vs *I was reading a book*.

points.title: I was talking to… : introducing news and background
points.summary: We use the past continuous to introduce news or a report of what someone said: *I was talking to Ali yesterday, and he told me…*

points.title: Regular verbs: -ed
points.summary: Add **-ed** to regular verbs: *work → worked, live → lived, study → studied, stop → stopped*. Same form for every person.

points.title: Irregular verbs
points.summary: Many common verbs have a special past form: *go → went, have → had, see → saw, buy → bought*. Learn them as words.

points.title: Didn't and did… ? (negatives and questions)
points.summary: Negative: **didn't + base verb**. Question: **Did + subject + base verb?** *I didn't go. Did you go?*

points.title: Time words: yesterday, last week, ago, in 2010
points.summary: Use the past simple with **finished** time: *yesterday, last Monday, two years ago, in 2010, when I was young*.

points.title: Telling a story: events in order
points.summary: Use the past simple for a series of finished events, one after another: *I got up, had a shower and left.*

points.title: Irregular verbs that are easy to mix up
points.summary: Some past forms look or sound similar: *fell / felt, thought / taught, bought / brought, left / lived, won / earned*.

points.title: Past forms that don't mean past
points.summary: The past simple can make requests softer (*I wondered if…*) and describe unreal situations (*It's time we left*).

points.title: Get up, turn on, put on, look for
points.summary: Everyday phrasal verbs: **get up, wake up, sit down, stand up, turn on / off, put on, take off, look for, come back, go out**. The particle changes the meaning.

points.title: Turn it off, not turn off it: separable verbs
points.summary: With many phrasal verbs, a **noun** can go **before or after** the particle (*turn off the TV / turn the TV off*), but a **pronoun** must go **in the middle**: *turn **it** off* (not *turn off it*).

points.title: Look after her, get on the bus: inseparable verbs
points.summary: Some phrasal verbs are **inseparable**: the object always goes **after** the particle, even a pronoun (*look after **her***, *come across **it***). Some have **no object** at all: *get up, grow up, break down*.

points.title: Look forward to, run out of, put up with
points.summary: **Three-part phrasal verbs** (verb + particle + preposition) can't be separated: **look forward to, get on with, run out of, put up with, come up with, catch up with, look up to, get away with, cut down on, keep up with**.

points.title: One phrasal verb, many meanings
points.summary: Many phrasal verbs have **several meanings**: *take off* (clothes / a plane / become successful), *pick up* (lift / collect / learn), *make up* (invent / become friends again), *work out* (exercise / solve), *put off* (postpone).

points.title: Particle meanings, phrasal nouns, and passives
points.summary: Particles often have a **general meaning** (*up* = completely, *out* = to the end or disappear, *on* = continue, *off* = stop or leave, *down* = decrease). Many phrasal verbs make **nouns** (*a breakdown, an outbreak, a setback*) and can be **passive** (*It was called off*).

points.title: Regular plurals: -s, -es, -ies, -ves
points.summary: Add **-s** to most nouns (*cars*). Add **-es** after *-s, -sh, -ch, -x* (*boxes*). Consonant + *y* → **-ies** (*cities*). Many *-f / -fe* words → **-ves** (*knives*).

points.title: Irregular plurals: men, children, feet, people
points.summary: Some common nouns have **irregular** plurals: *man → men, woman → women, child → children, person → people, foot → feet, tooth → teeth, mouse → mice*. Some don't change: *sheep, fish*.

points.title: Always plural: jeans, scissors, clothes, police
points.summary: Some nouns are **always plural**: *trousers, jeans, glasses, scissors, clothes*. Use **a pair of** to count them. ***Police*** and ***people*** also take a plural verb.

points.title: Group nouns: the team is or the team are?
points.summary: **Group nouns** like *family, team, government, staff, class* can take a **singular or plural verb** in British English (*The team is / are winning*). American English usually uses the singular.

points.title: Criteria, crises, passers-by and the news is
