points.summary: Greek and Latin plurals (*criterion → criteria, crisis → crises*), compound plurals (*passers-by*), nouns that are the same in the singular and plural (*series, species*), and singular nouns ending in *-s* (*news, physics*).

possessive-pronouns.h1: Possessive Pronouns: Mine, Yours, His, Hers

points.title: Mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs
points.summary: Use a **possessive pronoun** without a noun: *This phone is **mine**. Is this **yours**?* Use a **possessive adjective** before a noun: *This is **my** phone.*

points.title: Whose is it? Whose bag is this?
points.summary: Ask about the owner with ***whose***: *Whose bag is this?* or *Whose is this bag?* Answer with a possessive pronoun or *'s*: *It's **mine**. It's **Ali's**.*

points.title: My own, of my own, on my own
points.summary: ***Own*** emphasises possession: *my own room, a room of my own*. ***On my own*** = alone or without help (*I live on my own*). ***A friend of mine*** = one of my friends.

points.title: Formal possessives: one's own, whose for things, of which
points.summary: In formal English, use ***one's own*** for people in general. ***Whose*** can refer to **things** (*a company whose profits rose*), and ***of which*** is a formal alternative. Possessive pronouns avoid repeating a noun in comparisons: *Her results were better than **his***.

points.title: 's and s': my sister's car, my parents' house
points.summary: Add **'s** to a person or animal to show possession: *Ali's phone, my sister's car*. For regular plurals ending in *-s*, add only an **apostrophe**: *my parents' house*. Irregular plurals take **'s**: *the children's toys*.

points.title: At the doctor's, Ali and Sara's house
points.summary: Use **'s** for **shops and homes** without the noun: *at the doctor's, at my aunt's*. When two people **share** something, add *'s* to the **second** name: *Ali and Sara's flat*. For **separate** things, add it to both: *Ali's and Sara's phones*.

points.title: 's or of? My friend's name, the end of the film
points.summary: Use **'s** mostly for **people and animals** (*my friend's name*). Use **of** for **parts of things** (*the end of the street, the top of the page*). Both are possible with **places and organisations** (*Canada's capital / the capital of Canada*).

points.title: Today's news, a week's holiday, a friend of mine
points.summary: Use **'s / s'** with **time** expressions: *today's news, last week's meeting, a week's holiday, two hours' drive, in ten minutes' time*. Use **a friend of mine** or **a friend of my sister's** to mean *one of my friends*.

points.title: Group possessives, else's, its and one's
points.summary: **'s** can attach to a whole **noun phrase**: *the King of Spain's visit, someone else's bag*. In formal writing, prefer *of* with long phrases. Possessive pronouns have **no apostrophe**: *its, hers, ours, theirs*.

points.title: In, on, under, next to, between, behind
points.summary: Basic prepositions of place: ***in*** (inside), ***on*** (on a surface), ***under, next to, between, behind, in front of, opposite, near***.

points.title: In, on or at? At the door, in the room, on the wall
points.summary: ***At*** = a **point** or a place where something happens (*at the bus stop, at work, at a party*). ***In*** = **inside** an area or space (*in the kitchen, in Toronto*). ***On*** = a **surface** or a **line** (*on the wall, on the second floor*).

points.title: On the bus, in the car, arrive in or at
points.summary: Use ***on*** for public transport and bikes (*on the bus, on a plane, on my bike*) and ***in*** for cars and taxis (*in the car*). ***Arrive in*** a city or country; ***arrive at*** a building or place (*arrive at the airport*). Never *arrive to*.

points.title: Over, above, across, through, along, past
points.summary: ***Above / below*** = higher / lower. ***Over*** = above, often covering or moving to the other side. ***Across*** = from one side to the other of a flat surface. ***Through*** = inside, from one end to the other. ***Along*** = following a line. ***Past*** = going by.

points.title: Under pressure, on the brink of, beyond repair
points.summary: Prepositions of place are often used **figuratively**: ***under*** pressure / control / construction, ***on the verge / brink of***, ***beyond*** repair / belief, ***within*** reach / walking distance, ***among*** (in a group).

prepositions-of-time-in-on-at.h1: Prepositions of Time: In, On and At

points.title: At 6 o'clock, on Monday, in July
points.summary: ***At*** + times (*at 6 o'clock, at night*), ***on*** + days and dates (*on Monday, on 5 May*), ***in*** + months, years, seasons and parts of the day (*in July, in 2025, in the morning*).

points.title: On Monday morning, at night, in ten minutes, on time
points.summary: ***In the morning***, but ***on*** + a specific day: ***on Monday morning***. ***At night*** (in general), but ***in the night*** (during one night). ***In*** + period = after that time from now: *in ten minutes*. ***On time*** = not late; ***in time*** = early enough.

points.title: For, during or while?
points.summary: ***For*** + a period says **how long** (*for two hours*). ***During*** + a noun says **when**, inside a period (*during the film*). ***While*** + a clause (subject + verb): *while I was watching the film*.

points.title: By or until? From… to, within
points.summary: ***Until / till*** = up to a time (an action **continues**): *I'll wait **until** 6.* ***By*** = **not later than** (a deadline): *Please finish it **by** Friday.* ***Within*** = before the end of a period: *within 24 hours*.

points.title: As of, over the last decade, on arrival
points.summary: Formal and advanced expressions: ***as of / as from*** (starting from), ***over*** + period (during the whole period), ***in the run-up to*** (in the period before), ***in the course of*** (during), ***on*** + noun / *-ing* (as soon as), ***at the turn of the century***.

points.title: Form and use: I'm working (now)
points.summary: am / is / are + verb-ing for something happening at the moment of speaking.

points.title: Around now and temporary situations
points.summary: Use the present continuous for things happening around now (this week, at the moment) and temporary situations.

points.title: Future arrangements: I'm meeting Sam tonight
points.summary: Use the present continuous for future plans that are already arranged, usually with a time.

points.title: Changing situations: It's getting colder
points.summary: Use the present continuous for situations that are changing now: get, become, increase, improve.

points.title: always + continuous: He's always complaining
points.summary: always / constantly / forever + continuous for something that happens too often, often annoying.

points.title: In progress at a regular time; always for typical behaviour
points.summary: At 8 I'm usually driving = in the middle of it at that time; always + continuous can also describe typical (even positive) behaviour.

points.title: When not to use it for the future
points.summary: Use the present continuous for arranged or decided plans, not for predictions or permanent future situations.

present-perfect-continuous.h1: Present Perfect Continuous (I have been doing)

points.title: Form and use: still going on, how long
points.summary: **have / has been + -ing** for an activity that started in the past and continues now, often with *how long, for, since*.

points.title: An activity that has just stopped: evidence now
points.summary: We use it for an activity that has **recently stopped** when we can see the **result** now: *You're out of breath. Have you been running?*

points.title: Have been doing or have done?
points.summary: **have been doing** = the activity, how long, maybe not finished. **have done** = completed, a result, how many / how much.

points.title: Repeated actions and temporary situations
points.summary: The continuous can describe **repeated** actions over a period (*I've been going to the gym a lot*) and **temporary** situations (*I've been staying with friends*).

points.title: State verbs and verbs with two meanings
points.summary: State verbs use the **simple**: *I've known her for years.* Verbs like *have, think, see* can be continuous only in their action meaning: *I've been thinking about it.*

points.title: Subtle differences: temporary, unfinished, annoyed
points.summary: The continuous can make a situation sound **temporary**, **unfinished**, or **annoying**: *Who's been using my computer?* The simple sounds more **permanent** or **complete**.

points.title: Finished time or up to now?
points.summary: Past simple with a **finished time** (*yesterday, last week, in 2019, ago*). Present perfect when there's **no finished time** and the past is connected to now.

points.title: Have you ever…? Yes, I went there in…
points.summary: Use the present perfect to **ask about or introduce** an experience, then the past simple for the **details** (when, where, how).

points.title: Still true now, or finished?
points.summary: *I**'ve lived** here for ten years* = I still live here. *I **lived** there for ten years* = I don't now. People who are dead: past simple.

points.title: Today, this morning, this year: finished or not?
points.summary: *this morning, today, this week* take the present perfect if the period **isn't over** and the past simple if it **is over**.

points.title: American and British English
points.summary: In American English, the past simple is common with *just, already, yet* and *ever*: *I just ate. Did you finish yet?* British English prefers the present perfect.

points.title: When both are possible: the meaning changes
points.summary: Sometimes both tenses are correct, with a different focus: *I've always wanted* (still) vs *I always wanted* (not now); *Have you heard?* vs *Did you hear?*

points.title: Form: have / has + past participle
points.summary: **have / has + past participle**: *I've finished. She hasn't called. Have you eaten?*

points.title: Experiences: ever, never, before
points.summary: Use the present perfect for **life experiences** up to now, without saying when: *Have you ever been to Canada? I've never tried sushi.*

points.title: Just, already and yet
points.summary: **just** = a short time ago; **already** = sooner than expected; **yet** = up to now (in questions and negatives, at the end).

points.title: Been or gone?
points.summary: *She's **gone** to Paris* = she's there now. *She's **been** to Paris* = she went and came back.

points.title: A past action with a result now, and news
points.summary: The present perfect shows that a past action has a **result now** (*I've lost my keys* = I don't have them) and gives **new information**: *The prime minister has resigned.*

points.title: Today, this week, recently, so far
points.summary: Use the present perfect with periods of time that are **not finished**: *today, this week, this year, recently, lately, so far, up to now.*

points.title: It's the first time… and the best… I've ever…
points.summary: After *It's the first / second time* and after a superlative + *ever*, use the present perfect: *It's the first time I've driven. It's the best film I've ever seen.*

points.title: The present perfect in news and reports
points.summary: News and reports often **introduce** a topic with the present perfect and then give the **details** in the past simple: *A storm has hit the coast. It arrived at 3 am and destroyed…*

points.title: When I've finished…: the present perfect for the future
points.summary: In time clauses about the future, the present perfect shows that one action will be **complete** before another: *I'll call you when I've finished.*

points.title: Now or in general?
points.summary: Present continuous for now; present simple for habits, facts and things in general.

points.title: Temporary or permanent?
points.summary: Present continuous for temporary situations; present simple for permanent ones.

points.title: Stories, jokes and live commentary
points.summary: In informal stories and live commentary, the present continuous gives the background and the present simple gives the main events.

points.title: Form: I work, she works
points.summary: Use the base verb with I, you, we, they; add -s or -es with he, she, it.

points.title: Negatives and questions: don't, doesn't, do, does
points.summary: Negatives: don't / doesn't + base verb. Questions: do / does + subject + base verb.

points.title: Uses: habits, facts and permanent situations
points.summary: Use the present simple for habits, routines, facts, permanent situations and likes.

points.title: Timetables and schedules: The train leaves at 8
points.summary: Use the present simple for future events on a timetable or schedule.

points.title: I promise, I agree, I apologise: saying is doing
points.summary: Verbs like promise, agree and apologise do the action when you say them: use the present simple.

points.title: Headlines, summaries, instructions and I hear
points.summary: The present simple is also used in headlines, plot summaries, instructions and to pass on news (I hear, I gather).

quantifiers.h1: Quantifiers: All, Most, Each, Every, None

points.title: All, most, some, no: with or without of
points.summary: Use ***all / most / some / no*** + noun for things **in general** (*Most people like music*). Use ***all of / most of / some of / none of*** + ***the / my / these*** + noun, or a pronoun, for a **specific** group (*Most of my friends live here*).

points.title: Each or every?
points.summary: ***Each*** and ***every*** + **singular** noun + **singular** verb. ***Every*** = all of a group, seen together (*Every student passed*). ***Each*** = one by one, separately (*Each child got a present*). Only ***each*** can be used with ***of*** or alone.

points.title: Both, either, neither (of)
points.summary: For **two** things: ***both*** = the one and the other (+ plural); ***either*** = one or the other (+ singular); ***neither*** = not one and not the other (+ singular). With ***of***: *both of / either of / neither of* + ***the / my / them***.

points.title: All or whole? All, everything, no and none
points.summary: ***The whole*** + singular noun = all of one thing (*the whole day, the whole cake*). ***All*** goes with uncountable and plural nouns (*all the money, all the people*). ***Everything*** is more natural than *all* alone. ***None*** stands alone; ***no*** needs a noun.

points.title: None of them is or are? All of whom, each and every
points.summary: ***None of*** + plural takes a **singular** verb in formal style and a **plural** verb in everyday English. In relative clauses, use ***all / most / none / both of whom / which***. ***Each and every*** is emphatic. ***Not all*** ≠ ***none***.

question-tags.h1: Question Tags (…, isn't it? …, don't you?)

points.title: Positive sentence, negative tag (and the other way)
points.summary: Positive + negative tag: *You're Iranian, **aren't you**?* Negative + positive tag: *She doesn't eat meat, **does she**?* Use the same auxiliary as the sentence.

points.title: Intonation: a real question or asking for agreement?
points.summary: **Rising** intonation (↗) = a real question, I'm not sure. **Falling** intonation (↘) = I'm sure, I want you to agree.

points.title: Special tags: aren't I, let's… shall we, imperatives, there is
points.summary: **I am → aren't I?** **Let's → shall we?** Imperatives → **will you? / won't you? / can you?** **There is → isn't there?** **Everybody → they**.

points.title: Never, hardly, no one: negative words take a positive tag
points.summary: Sentences with **never, hardly, rarely, no, nobody, nothing** are negative, so the tag is **positive**: *You never call me, **do you**?*

points.title: Same-way tags and tags in requests
points.summary: **Positive + positive** tags show surprise, interest or irony: *So you're the new boss, **are you**?* Negative sentence + positive tag in polite requests: *You couldn't help me, **could you**?*

points.title: Yes/no questions: Are you…? Do you…? Can you…?
points.summary: Put **be** or an **auxiliary** (*do, does, did, can, will, have*) before the subject: *Are you ready? Does she work here? Can you swim?*

points.title: Wh- question words: what, where, when, who, why, how
points.summary: Put the question word **first**, then the auxiliary and the subject: *Where do you live? What is your name? Why did she leave?*

points.title: How much, how many, how long, how often, how far
points.summary: **How + adjective / adverb** asks about amount, time and frequency: *How much is it? How long does it take? How often do you exercise?*

points.title: Who saw you? or Who did you see? Subject and object questions
points.summary: When **who / what** is the **subject**, don't use *do / did*: *Who called you?* When it's the **object**, use *do / did*: *Who did you call?*

points.title: Who is she talking to? What is it like? Prepositions at the end
points.summary: In questions, prepositions usually go at the **end**: *Who are you talking **to**? Where are you **from**?* **What is it like?** = describe it.

points.title: What or which? What kind of…?
points.summary: **which** = a choice from a small, known group: *Which colour do you want, red or blue?* **what** = an open choice: *What colour is your car?*

points.title: Negative questions: Don't you…? Isn't it…?
points.summary: Negative questions (*Don't you…? Isn't it…? Haven't you…?*) show **surprise**, ask for **agreement**, or check something we **expect** to be true.

points.title: Echo questions and statement questions: You did what?
points.summary: **Echo questions** repeat part of what someone said to show surprise or check: *She's moving to Peru. ~ She's moving where?* **Statement questions** keep normal word order with rising intonation: *You're leaving?*

points.title: A bit, fairly, quite, very: how strong?
points.summary: From weaker to stronger: ***a bit / a little*** < ***fairly*** < ***quite / pretty*** < ***very / really*** < ***extremely***.

points.title: Quite: fairly or completely?
points.summary: With most adjectives, ***quite*** = **fairly** (*quite good*). With **extreme** or **absolute** adjectives (*amazing, impossible, sure, right*), ***quite*** = **completely** (*quite impossible, quite right*). ***Quite a lot / quite a few*** = a fairly large amount.

points.title: Rather and pretty: rather expensive, pretty good
points.summary: ***Rather*** is like *quite*, but it often sounds **negative** or **surprised**: *It's rather expensive.* With positive words, it means *surprisingly*: *The film was rather good.* ***Pretty*** is informal: *pretty good, pretty tired*.

points.title: Somewhat, relatively, reasonably: formal alternatives
points.summary: In formal English, use ***somewhat, slightly, reasonably, moderately*** and ***relatively*** instead of *a bit, quite* or *pretty*: *The results were **somewhat** disappointing. Prices are **relatively** low.* ***Rather*** and ***quite*** can also go with verbs: *I **rather** like it. I **quite** understand.*

points.title: Myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, themselves
points.summary: Use a **reflexive pronoun** when the **subject and object are the same**: *I hurt **myself**. They enjoyed **themselves**.*

points.title: Enjoy yourself, help yourself, by myself; relax, feel, meet
points.summary: Some verbs often take a reflexive pronoun: ***enjoy yourself, help yourself, behave yourself, introduce yourself***. Many verbs usually **don't** in English: *relax, feel, concentrate, meet, wash, get dressed*. ***By myself*** = alone.

points.title: Each other and one another
points.summary: Use ***each other*** (or ***one another***) when two or more people do something **to the other(s)**: *Ali and Sara love **each other**.* Compare: *They blamed **themselves*** (each blamed himself or herself) / *They blamed **each other*** (A blamed B, and B blamed A).

points.title: Emphatic myself: I did it myself
points.summary: Use a reflexive pronoun for **emphasis**: *I made the cake **myself*** (= I made it, not someone else). *The manager **herself** called me* (= the manager, not her assistant).

points.title: Me or myself? Reflexives after prepositions
points.summary: Don't use ***myself*** instead of ***me / I*** to sound polite: *Please contact **me*** (not *contact myself*). After **prepositions of place**, use an **object pronoun**: *She put the bag **beside her***. Use a reflexive when the object is the same person as the subject: *He's talking **to himself***.

points.title: Say or tell? She said / She told me
points.summary: **say** + (that) + what: *She said (that) she was hungry.* **tell + person** + (that): *She told me (that) she was hungry.*

points.title: Tense changes: one step back
points.summary: When the reporting verb is past (*said, told*), the tense usually moves **one step back**: *“I'm tired” → She said she **was** tired. “I'll call” → He said he **would** call.*

points.title: When the tense doesn't change
points.summary: Don't change the tense when the reporting verb is **present** (*She says she's tired*) or, optionally, when the situation is **still true**: *He said he lives in Paris.*

points.title: Time and place words: tomorrow → the next day
points.summary: When the time or place has changed, words like **now, today, tomorrow, here, this** change too: *“I'll see you tomorrow.” → He said he'd see me **the next day**.*

points.title: Reported questions: He asked me where I lived
points.summary: Reported questions use **statement word order** and no *do / did*: *“Where do you live?” → He asked me where I **lived**.* Yes/no questions use **if / whether**.

points.title: Reported orders and requests: told me to, asked me not to
points.summary: **tell / ask + person + (not) to + verb**: *“Sit down.” → She told me **to sit** down. “Please don't shout.” → He asked us **not to** shout.*

points.title: Modals in reported speech
points.summary: **can → could, will → would, may → might, must → had to / must**. **Could, would, should, might, ought to** don't change.

points.title: Choosing the tense: reporting news, facts and opinions
points.summary: Backshift is not automatic. Choose the tense to show if something is **still true**, and use **present** reporting verbs for news, written sources and opinions: *The report says…*

reporting-verbs.h1: Reporting Verbs (She promised to…, He denied…)

points.title: Verb + to: agree, offer, promise, refuse, threaten
points.summary: **agree / offer / promise / refuse / threaten / decide / claim + to + verb**: *He offered to help me. She refused to answer.*

points.title: Verb + object + to: advise, remind, warn, encourage, invite
points.summary: **advise / ask / tell / remind / warn / encourage / invite / persuade / order + person + to + verb**: *She reminded me to call my mum.*

points.title: Verb + -ing and verb + preposition + -ing: deny, admit, apologise for, accuse of
points.summary: **deny / admit / recommend / mention + -ing**. **apologise for / insist on / blame for / accuse of / congratulate on / thank for + -ing**.

points.title: Verb + that: explain, admit, claim, complain, agree, insist
points.summary: **explain / admit / claim / complain / agree / insist / point out / announce + (that) + clause**: *She explained that the train was late.*

points.title: Suggest and recommend: the right patterns
points.summary: **suggest / recommend + -ing**, **+ (that) + someone + (should) + verb**, or **+ noun**. Not *suggest someone to do*.

points.title: Reporting with nouns and adjectives: the claim that, her refusal to
points.summary: Many reporting verbs have noun forms with the same patterns: **the claim that…, her refusal to…, his insistence on…, my suggestion that…**. Adjectives too: **sure that, aware that, adamant that**.

requests-offers-permission.h1: Requests, Offers and Permission (Can you…? May I…? Shall I…?)

points.title: Can you…? Could you…? Asking someone to do something
points.summary: **Can you…?** and **Could you…?** + base verb ask someone to do something. *Could* is more polite: *Could you close the door, please?*

points.title: Can I…? Could I…? May I…? Asking for permission
points.summary: **Can I…?** (informal), **Could I…?** (polite) and **May I…?** (formal) ask for permission: *May I come in?*

points.title: Offers and suggestions: Shall I…? Shall we…? Would you like…?
points.summary: Offers: **Shall I…? / Can I…? / I'll…** Suggestions: **Shall we…? / Let's… / Why don't we…?** Invitations: **Would you like…?**

points.title: Would you mind…? Do you mind if…?
points.summary: **Would you mind + -ing?** = a polite request. **Do you mind if I + present / Would you mind if I + past** = asking for permission. Answer *No, not at all* to say yes!

points.title: Be allowed to: permission and rules
points.summary: **be allowed to + verb** = have permission: *We **are allowed to** use phones at break.* Past: **was allowed to** / **could** (general). Rules: **not allowed to**.

points.title: Very polite requests: I was wondering if…, Would it be possible…?
points.summary: Indirect forms make requests softer and more formal: *I was wondering if you could…, Would it be possible to…?, Do you think you could…?, I'd appreciate it if you could…*

second-conditional.h1: Second Conditional (If I had…, I would…)

points.title: Form and use: if + past simple, would + verb
points.summary: **if + past simple, would + base verb** for an imaginary or unlikely situation: *If I won the lottery, I'd travel the world.*

points.title: What would you do if…?
points.summary: Questions: **What would you do if** you lost your phone? Short answers: *Yes, I would. / No, I wouldn't.*

points.title: First or second conditional?
points.summary: First = a **real** possibility (*If I win, I'll…*). Second = **imaginary or unlikely** (*If I won, I'd…*). The speaker chooses.

points.title: Could and might in the second conditional
points.summary: Use **could** (= would be able to) or **might** (= perhaps would) in the result: *If I had time, I **could** help.* *If I could…* in the *if* clause = if I was able to.

points.title: Giving advice: If I were you…
points.summary: **If I were you, I'd…** gives advice. *I'd…* alone, or *If I were in your position…*, also work.

points.title: If I were to…, If it weren't for…
points.summary: **If + were to + verb** makes a future situation more hypothetical or polite. **If it weren't for…** = without…

should-have-could-have-neednt-have.h1: Should Have, Could Have, Would Have, Needn't Have

points.title: Should have / shouldn't have: regrets and criticism
points.summary: **should have + past participle** = it was a good idea, but it didn't happen. **shouldn't have** = it happened, but it was a mistake.

points.title: Could have: a chance you didn't take
points.summary: **could have + past participle** = it was possible, but it didn't happen: *I **could have** gone to university, but I started working.*

points.title: Would have: what you were willing to do
points.summary: **would have + past participle** = you were ready or willing to do something, but it didn't happen: *I **would have** helped you, but you didn't ask.*

points.title: Needn't have or didn't need to?
points.summary: **needn't have + past participle** = you did it, but it wasn't necessary. **didn't need to** = it wasn't necessary (you probably didn't do it).

points.title: You shouldn't have!, should have for expectations, might have for annoyance
points.summary: *You **shouldn't have**!* = a polite thank you for a gift. *They **should have** arrived by now* = expected. *You **might have** warned me!* = annoyance.

should-ought-to.h1: Should, Ought To and Had Better

points.title: Should and shouldn't for advice
points.summary: **should / shouldn't + base verb** for advice and opinions: *You **should** go to bed earlier. You **shouldn't** eat so much sugar.*

points.title: Ought to
points.summary: **ought to + base verb** = should. It's a little more formal and is less common in questions and negatives: *You **ought to** call your mother.*

points.title: Had better: strong advice and warnings
points.summary: **had better ('d better) + base verb** = strong advice for a particular situation, often with a warning: *You**'d better** hurry or you'll miss the train.*

points.title: Should for expectations: It should arrive tomorrow
points.summary: **should** also means *probably will* or *is expected to*: *The package **should** arrive tomorrow. They **should** be here by now.*

points.title: Be supposed to
points.summary: **be supposed to + verb** = what is expected, arranged or the rule (often not what really happens): *We're **supposed to** wear a tie. You **were supposed to** call me!*

points.title: Should in that-clauses and for surprise
points.summary: After verbs like **suggest, insist, recommend** and adjectives like **important, essential**, British English often uses **should**: *I suggest that you **should** apply.* **Should** also shows surprise: *It's strange that she **should** say that.*

so-do-i-neither-do-i.h1: Short Answers, So Do I, Neither Do I, I Think So

points.title: Short answers: Yes, I do. No, she isn't.
points.summary: Answer yes/no questions with **Yes / No + pronoun + auxiliary**: *Are you hungry? ~ Yes, I **am**. Do they live here? ~ No, they **don't**.*

points.title: So do I, Neither can I, Me too, Me neither
points.summary: To agree: **So + auxiliary + I** (positive): *I'm hungry. ~ So am I.* **Neither + auxiliary + I** (negative): *I can't swim. ~ Neither can I.*

points.title: Reply questions: Have you? Really? Is she?
points.summary: Short **reply questions** (*Have you? Did she? Is it?*) show interest or surprise: *I've just got married! ~ Have you? Congratulations!*

points.title: I think so, I hope so, I'm afraid not, I don't think so
points.summary: Use **so** / **not** instead of repeating a clause: *Is it going to rain? ~ I hope not. Will she come? ~ I think so.*

points.title: Using auxiliaries to avoid repetition: She can, but I can't
points.summary: Use an **auxiliary** alone to avoid repeating a verb phrase: *I haven't seen it, but my brother **has**. She speaks French and **so does** her son.*

points.title: Nor, so it is, and other auxiliary patterns
points.summary: **Nor** + inversion adds a negative point formally (*He didn't apologise, nor did he explain*). **So it is / So I did** confirms with surprise. Stressed **do** adds emphasis (*I do like it!*).

points.title: So or such? So hot, such a hot day
points.summary: Use ***so*** + adjective or adverb (*so tired, so quickly*). Use ***such*** + (*a / an*) + (adjective) + noun (*such a nice man, such good weather*).

points.title: So… that, such… that: results
points.summary: ***so*** + adjective + ***that*** and ***such*** + noun phrase + ***that*** show a **result**: *It was so cold that we stayed inside. It was such a cold day that we stayed inside.* *That* can be left out in informal English.

points.title: So (result) or so that (purpose)?
points.summary: ***so*** + clause = **result** (*It was late, so I took a taxi*). ***so that*** + clause, often with *can / could*, = **purpose** (*I took a taxi so that I wouldn't be late*).

points.title: So good a book, such was the demand, so loud was the music
points.summary: Formal patterns: ***so*** + adjective + ***a*** + noun (*so good a book*), ***Such*** + *be* at the start with inversion (*Such was the noise that…*), ***So*** + adjective + *be* + subject (*So strong was the wind that…*), and ***such that*** (= in a way that).

points.title: Some in positive sentences, any in negatives and questions
points.summary: Use ***some*** in **positive** sentences (*I've got some apples*). Use ***any*** in **negatives** (*I haven't got any apples*) and most **questions** (*Have you got any apples?*).

points.title: Some in offers and requests: Can I have some water?
points.summary: Use ***some*** in **questions** when you **offer** something or **ask for** something, or when you expect the answer *yes*: *Would you like **some** coffee? Can I have **some** water?*

points.title: Someone, anything, nowhere, everybody
points.summary: ***Some-, any-, no-, every-*** combine with ***-one / -body*** (people), ***-thing*** (things) and ***-where*** (places): *someone, anything, nowhere, everybody*. Use them like *some* and *any*.

points.title: Any = it doesn't matter which; any after if
points.summary: In **positive** sentences, ***any*** means **it doesn't matter which**: *Call me **any** time.* Use ***any*** after ***if*** and with words that have a **negative meaning** (*never, hardly, without*).

points.title: Some 200 people, some idiot, any better, no faster
points.summary: ***Some*** + number = **about** (*some 200 people*). ***Some*** + singular noun = an **unknown** person or thing (*Some idiot parked in my space*). ***Any / no*** + comparative = *at all* (*Is he any better? It's no faster.*).

points.title: Verbs we don't use in the continuous
points.summary: know, want, like, need, understand, believe, belong… use the simple form, even for now.

points.title: Verbs with two meanings: think, have, see, taste
points.summary: Some verbs are states with one meaning and actions with another; only the action meaning can be continuous.

points.title: He's being rude: be in the continuous, and states in perfect tenses
points.summary: is being + adjective = behaviour right now; state verbs stay simple in perfect tenses (I've known, not I've been knowing).

points.title: State verbs in the continuous for emphasis or change
points.summary: Informally, some state verbs take the continuous to stress a temporary feeling or a gradual change: We're loving it, I'm regretting it.

still-yet-already.h1: Still, Yet, Already, Any More and No Longer

points.title: Still, yet, already
points.summary: ***Still*** = continuing (*It's still raining*). ***Already*** = sooner than expected (*I've already finished*). ***Yet*** = until now, in **negatives and questions** (*Has she called yet? She hasn't called yet.*)

points.title: Still not, not yet, already in questions
points.summary: ***Still*** in negatives shows **surprise or impatience**: *He **still** hasn't called!* ***Not… yet*** is neutral: *He hasn't called **yet**.* ***Already*** in a question shows **surprise** that something happened early: *Have you finished **already**?*

points.title: Not any more, not any longer, no longer
points.summary: Use ***not… any more / any longer*** (or formal ***no longer***) for something that **stopped**: *I don't live there **any more**. She **no longer** works here.* The opposite is ***still***.

points.title: Formal yet and still: has yet to, as yet, still harder
points.summary: Formal uses: ***have yet to*** + verb = haven't … yet (*The results have yet to be published*); ***as yet*** = until now; ***(and) yet*** = but; ***Still,…*** = even so; ***still*** + comparative = even (*still harder*); superlative + ***yet*** = so far (*her best work yet*).

points.title: Subject pronouns: I, you, he, she, it, we, they
points.summary: Use a **subject pronoun** before the verb: *I, you, he, she, it, we, they*. English sentences **need** a subject: *It's raining.* (not *Is raining*)

points.title: Possessive adjectives: my, your, his, her, its, our, their
points.summary: Use **possessive adjectives** before a noun to show who something belongs to: *my bag, your phone, his car, her house, its tail, our school, their children*.

points.title: Its or it's? Their, there or they're? Your or you're?
points.summary: Don't confuse possessive adjectives with short forms: ***its*** (possessive) / ***it's*** (= it is / it has); ***their*** (possessive) / ***there*** (place) / ***they're*** (= they are); ***your*** / ***you're*** (= you are).

points.title: It for weather, time and distance; it as an empty subject
points.summary: Use ***it*** as an **empty subject** for weather, time, dates and distance (*It's raining. It's 5 o'clock. It's 10 km to the city.*), before *adjective + to / that* (*It's important to sleep well*), and with ***it takes*** + time.

points.title: Singular they, generic you and one
points.summary: Use ***they / their*** for **one person** when you don't know, or don't want to say, if the person is male or female: *Someone left **their** phone.* Use ***you*** (informal) or ***one*** (very formal) for **people in general**: *You never know.*

points.title: He works, they work; there is, there are
points.summary: In the present, use **-s** with *he, she, it* and singular nouns (*My brother works*). With *I, you, we, they* and plural nouns, there's no *-s* (*My brothers work*). Use **there is** + singular and **there are** + plural.

points.title: Everyone is, each student has, one of my friends is
points.summary: ***Everyone, everybody, someone, nobody, everything*** take a **singular** verb (*Everyone is here*). So do ***each*** and ***every*** + noun. ***One of*** + plural noun also takes a **singular** verb (*One of my friends lives in Paris*).

points.title: Long subjects: the list of names is, either… or
points.summary: The verb agrees with the **main noun** of the subject, not the noun closest to it: *The list of names **is** on the wall.* With ***as well as / along with***, it agrees with the **first** subject. With ***either… or / neither… nor***, it agrees with the **nearest** subject.

points.title: Amounts, what-clauses and none of them is or are
points.summary: **Amounts** of money, time and distance usually take a **singular** verb (*Ten dollars is enough*). ***What***-clauses usually take a singular verb (*What we need is more time*). With ***none of*** + plural, both singular and plural are used.

subjunctive.h1: The Subjunctive (I Insist That He Be…)

points.title: Suggest that he see, insist that she be
points.summary: After ***suggest, recommend, insist, demand, request, propose, ask*** + ***that***, use the **base form** for every person: *They insisted **that he leave**. I recommend **that she be** careful.* British English also uses ***should*** + base form.

points.title: It's essential that he be…, it's vital that
points.summary: After ***essential, vital, important, crucial, imperative, necessary, advisable*** + ***that***, formal English uses the **subjunctive** (base form): ***It is essential that** every child **have** access to education.* Also after nouns like ***the suggestion / requirement / insistence that***.

points.title: That he not be told, that it be done
points.summary: The **negative** subjunctive is ***not*** + base form (no *do*): *I suggest that he **not go**.* The **passive** subjunctive is ***be*** + past participle: *They demanded that the law **be changed**.*

points.title: If I were you, I wish it were, as if he were
points.summary: The ***were*** subjunctive is used for **unreal** situations with **all** persons, especially after ***if, I wish, if only, as if / as though, suppose***: *If I **were** you… I wish he **were** here. He acts as if he **were** the boss.* In informal English, *was* is also common.

points.title: If need be, as it were, heaven forbid, long live
points.summary: Some **fixed expressions** keep old subjunctive forms: ***if need be*** (= if necessary), ***as it were*** (= so to speak), ***heaven forbid*** (= I hope it never happens), ***long live…***, ***God bless***, ***woe betide***, ***the powers that be***.

points.title: General or specific? Music or the music
points.summary: No article for things **in general** (plural and uncountable nouns): *I love music. Cats are clever.* Use **the** for **specific** things: *The music at the party was great.*

points.title: At home, go to work, in bed, by bus, have lunch
points.summary: No article in fixed phrases with **home, work, school, bed, hospital, prison, church, university**, with **meals** (*have breakfast*) and with **by + transport** (*by bus*).

points.title: Countries, cities, rivers and mountains
points.summary: No article for most **countries, cities, streets, lakes, single mountains and continents** (*Canada, Lake Ontario, Mount Everest*). Use **the** for **rivers, seas, oceans, mountain ranges, island groups, deserts** and plural names (*the Nile, the Alps, the USA*).

points.title: Names of buildings, organisations and newspapers
points.summary: Use **the** with hotels, museums, theatres, newspapers and names with **of** (*the Hilton, the Louvre, the Guardian, the University of Toronto*). No article with **place name + airport / station / university / park** (*Pearson Airport, Oxford University, Central Park*) or company names.

points.title: Fixed pairs, roles, headlines and decades
points.summary: No article in **fixed pairs** (*arm in arm, from start to finish*), for **unique roles** after verbs like *elect, appoint, become* (*She became CEO*), and in **headlines**. Use **the** for decades (*the 1990s*), and say **at night** (in general) but **in the night** (one night).

points.title: There's a…, there are some…
points.summary: ***There is / There's*** + **singular** or **uncountable** noun. ***There are*** + **plural** noun: ***There's** a sofa. **There's** some milk. **There are** two chairs.*

points.title: There isn't, there aren't any; Is there…?
points.summary: **Negative**: ***There isn't a… / There isn't any…*** (uncountable), ***There aren't any…*** (plural). **Questions**: ***Is there a…? Are there any…?*** Short answers: *Yes, there is. No, there aren't.*

points.title: There was, there were, there will be, there has been
points.summary: Change ***be*** for other tenses: ***there was / were*** (past), ***there will be*** / ***there's going to be*** (future), ***there has / have been*** (present perfect).

points.title: There must be, there seems to be, there used to be
points.summary: ***There*** works with **modals** and other verbs: ***there must / might / could / should be***, ***there seems / appears to be***, ***there used to be***, ***there's bound / likely to be***.

points.title: There's no point in, there's no need to, for there to be
points.summary: Fixed patterns: ***There's no point (in)*** + *-ing*, ***There's no need to*** + verb, ***There's no way*** + clause, ***There's nothing like…***, ***for there to be***, and formal ***there is said / thought to be***.

third-conditional.h1: Third Conditional (If I had known…, I would have…)

points.title: Form and use: if + past perfect, would have + past participle
points.summary: **if + had + past participle, would have + past participle** for an imaginary past: *If we had left earlier, we would have caught the train.*

points.title: 'd = had or would? Contractions in the third conditional
points.summary: In *If I'd known, I'd have called*, the first **'d = had**, the second **'d = would**. *'d* + past participle = had; *'d have* = would have.

points.title: Could have, might have in the result
points.summary: **could have** + past participle = would have been able to; **might have** = perhaps would have: *If you'd asked, I could have helped.*

points.title: Continuous forms: If I hadn't been driving so fast…
points.summary: Use **had been + -ing** or **would have been + -ing** for actions in progress: *If I hadn't been driving so fast, I wouldn't have crashed.*

points.title: If it hadn't been for…, But for…, Without…
points.summary: **If it hadn't been for** + noun = without this thing, the past would have been different: *If it hadn't been for you, I'd have failed.*

points.title: This, that, these, those: near and far
points.summary: ***This*** + singular and ***these*** + plural = **near**. ***That*** + singular and ***those*** + plural = **far**.

points.title: This is…, that's great, this one
points.summary: Use ***this*** to introduce people (*This is my friend*) and on the phone (*Hi, this is Sara*). ***That's*** reacts to what someone has just said (*That's great!*). ***This one / that one*** replace a noun.

points.title: This morning, that day, these days, in those days
points.summary: ***This*** + time = the **present** or a **near** time (*this morning, this week*). ***That*** + time = a **past** time we've mentioned (*that day, that night*). ***These days*** = nowadays; ***in those days*** = at that time in the past.

points.title: This and that in writing: this means, those who
points.summary: In writing, ***this*** often refers to an idea **just mentioned** (*This means that…*). ***That*** refers to what another person said. ***Those who*** = the people who; ***that of / those of*** replace a noun (*higher than those of last year*).

points.title: Storytelling this, shared that, and not that hungry
points.summary: In informal stories, ***this*** introduces something **new** (*So this man comes up to me…*). ***That*** refers to **shared memories** or shows dislike (*Remember that café? I hate that noise.*). ***That*** + adjective = *very / so* (*I'm not that hungry*).

points.title: When, while, before, after
points.summary: ***When*** = at that time. ***While*** = during a longer action (often with the past continuous). ***Before*** and ***after*** show the order. The time clause can go **first** (with a comma) or **second**.

points.title: As soon as, until, since, once, by the time
points.summary: ***As soon as*** = immediately after. ***Until*** = up to that time. ***Since*** = from that time to now (with the present perfect). ***Once*** = after (when something is finished). ***By the time*** = before or at the moment that.

points.title: First, then, after that, finally, in the end, at last
points.summary: To tell a story or give instructions in order: ***first***, ***then / next / after that***, ***finally***. ***In the end*** = after a long time or many changes. ***At last*** = after waiting a long time (relief). ***Eventually*** = after a long time.

points.title: The moment, every time, as, whenever
points.summary: ***The moment / the minute*** = as soon as. ***Every time / whenever*** = each time. ***As*** = at the same time as (two things changing or happening together). ***Hardly … when*** = something happened immediately after.

points.title: No sooner … than, upon arrival, prior to, following
points.summary: Formal time expressions: ***no sooner … than*** and ***hardly / scarcely … when*** (often with inversion), ***upon / on*** + *-ing* or noun, ***prior to***, ***following***, ***having*** + past participle.

points.title: Too hot, warm enough, enough money
points.summary: Use ***too*** + adjective or adverb (*too expensive*), adjective or adverb + ***enough*** (*big enough*), and ***enough*** + noun (*enough time*).

points.title: Too much, too many, too difficult for me to do
points.summary: Use ***too much*** + uncountable noun and ***too many*** + plural noun. Use ***too / enough*** + ***(for someone)*** + ***to***-infinitive: *It's too cold (for us) to swim. She's old enough to vote.*

points.title: Far too, more than enough, sufficiently, overly
points.summary: Make ***too*** stronger with ***far / much / way*** (*far too expensive*). ***More than enough*** = plenty. Formal English uses ***sufficiently*** (= enough) and ***overly / excessively*** (= too).

unreal-past.h1: Unreal Past (It's time we went, I'd rather you didn't…)

points.title: It's time…: it's time to go, it's time we went
points.summary: **It's time + to-infinitive** or **It's time + subject + past simple**: *It's time to go. It's time we went.* **High / about time** = it should have happened already.

points.title: Would rather: I'd rather stay, I'd rather you stayed
points.summary: **would rather + base verb** (your own preference). **would rather + another person + past simple** (what you want someone else to do).

points.title: As if / as though: real or unreal?
points.summary: **as if / as though** + present for something that seems **true** (*It looks as if it's going to rain*). + past for something **unreal** (*He talks as if he knew everything*).

points.title: Suppose, supposing, imagine, what if
points.summary: **suppose / supposing / imagine / what if** + present = a real possibility. + past = an imaginary or less likely situation. + past perfect = an imaginary past.

points.title: Unreal past about the past: past perfect
points.summary: To talk about an unreal **past**, use the **past perfect**: *I'd rather you **hadn't told** him. He looked as if he **had seen** a ghost.*

points.title: Used to: past habits and states
points.summary: **used to + base verb** for something that was true or happened regularly in the past but doesn't now.

points.title: Didn't use to and Did you use to…?
points.summary: Negative: **didn't use to**. Question: **Did … use to…?** (no *d* after *did*).

points.title: Used to or past simple?
points.summary: Use *used to* for repeated actions or long situations. Use the **past simple** for one action, a number of times, or an exact length of time.

points.title: Used to do or be used to doing?
points.summary: *I **used to work** at night* = in the past (not now). *I**'m used to working** at night* = it's normal for me, not strange.

points.title: Would for past habits
points.summary: **would** + base verb can describe repeated **actions** in the past, especially in stories: *Every summer we would go to the lake.* Not for states.

points.title: Will and would for typical behaviour
points.summary: **will / would** can describe typical or characteristic behaviour: *She'll sit there for hours.* Stressed **would** can show criticism: *He WOULD say that!*

verb-to-be.h1: The Verb To Be (Am, Is, Are)

points.title: I am, you are, he is: forms and contractions
points.summary: ***I am*** (I'm), ***you / we / they are*** ('re), ***he / she / it is*** ('s). In speaking, we usually use the **short forms**.

points.title: I'm not, isn't, aren't; Are you…?
points.summary: **Negative**: ***I'm not, he isn't (is not), they aren't (are not)***. **Questions**: put *be* first: ***Are** you OK? **Is** she here?* Short answers: *Yes, I am. No, she isn't.*

points.title: I'm 25, I'm hungry, I'm cold: be, not have
points.summary: English uses ***be*** (not *have*) for **age** (*I'm 25*), **feelings** (*I'm hungry, I'm cold, I'm afraid*), **jobs** (*She's a doctor*), **nationality**, and **be born** (*I was born in 1990*).

points.title: I agree, not I'm agree: be or do?
points.summary: Don't use ***be*** with other verbs in the present simple: *I **agree*** (not *I'm agree*), *I **don't understand*** (not *I'm not understand*), ***Do** you like…?* (not *Are you like…?*). Use ***be*** with **adjectives**, **nouns** and **-ing**.

points.title: He's being silly: be in the continuous
points.summary: ***Be*** can be continuous (***am / is / are being***) to talk about **temporary behaviour**: *You're **being** very rude today.* (= you're acting rudely now). It's also used in the **passive continuous**: *The road **is being** repaired.*

points.title: Listen to, wait for, look at, depend on
points.summary: Common pairs: **listen to**, **wait for**, **look at**, **ask for**, **pay for**, **talk to / about**, **think about**, **belong to**, **depend on**, **agree with**.

points.title: Discuss, enter, marry, call: no preposition
points.summary: Some verbs take a **direct object** with **no preposition**: **discuss** a problem, **enter** a room, **marry** someone, **call / phone** someone, **answer** a question, **reach** a place, **approach** someone, **lack** something.

points.title: Thank someone for, remind someone of, spend money on
points.summary: **Verb + object + preposition**: **thank / blame** someone **for**, **accuse** someone **of**, **remind** someone **of / about**, **spend** money **on**, **provide** someone **with**, **protect / prevent** someone **from**, **congratulate** someone **on**, **borrow** something **from**.

points.title: Look at, look for, look after; think of or about
points.summary: The **preposition** can change the **meaning**: *look **at** / **for** / **after***, *think **of** / **about***, *hear **about** / **of** / **from***, *care **about** / **for***, *agree **with** / **to** / **on***, *dream **of** / **about***.

points.title: Comply with, refrain from, account for, attribute to
points.summary: Formal verb + preposition pairs: **comply with**, **adhere to**, **abide by**, **refrain from**, **account for**, **attribute** something **to**, **cope / contend with**, **object to + -ing**, **capitalise on**, **embark on**, **dispose of**.

verbs-change-meaning-ing-infinitive.h1: Verbs that Change Meaning with -ing or To

points.title: Like, love, start, begin, continue: little or no difference
points.summary: **like, love, hate, prefer, start, begin, continue** can take **-ing** or **to** with little difference: *It started raining / to rain.*

points.title: Remember and forget: -ing or to?
points.summary: **remember / forget + -ing** = a memory of the past. **remember / forget + to** = a duty, something you need to do (before you do it).

points.title: Stop and go on: -ing or to?
points.summary: **stop + -ing** = not do it any more. **stop + to** = stop one thing in order to do another. **go on + -ing** = continue. **go on + to** = do something next.

points.title: Try and need: -ing or to?
points.summary: **try + to** = make an effort (it's difficult). **try + -ing** = do it as an experiment to see if it works. **need + to** = it's necessary for me. **need + -ing** = it needs to be done (passive meaning).

points.title: Regret and mean: -ing or to?
points.summary: **regret + -ing** = be sorry about something you did. **regret + to** = be sorry to give bad news (formal). **mean + -ing** = involve. **mean + to** = intend.

points.title: Afraid to or afraid of -ing? Sorry to or sorry for -ing?
points.summary: **afraid to do** = you don't do it because it's dangerous or scary. **afraid of doing** = afraid that something might happen. **sorry to** = sorry about now. **sorry for / about -ing** = sorry about the past.

points.title: I was, you were: the forms
points.summary: I / he / she / it **was**; you / we / they **were**.

points.title: Wasn't, weren't and questions
points.summary: Negative: **wasn't / weren't**. Questions: **Was** he…? **Were** you…? No *did*.

points.title: Was born, was / were + adjective, it was
points.summary: *I **was born** in 1995.* (not *I born*). Use *was / were* to describe the past: *It was cold. They were nervous.*

points.title: Was / were or did?
points.summary: *Was / were* + adjective, noun, place or *-ing*. *Did* + base verb. Don't mix them.

points.title: Were after if and wish: If I were you…
points.summary: In unreal sentences we often use **were** for all persons: *If I **were** you… I wish it **were** Friday.*

points.title: Will and won't: form and future facts
points.summary: **will / won't + base verb**, the same for every person: *I'll be 30 next year. She won't be here tomorrow.*

points.title: Instant decisions, offers, promises and requests
points.summary: Use **will** when you decide at the moment of speaking (*I'll have the soup*), and for offers (*I'll help*), promises (*I'll call you*) and requests (*Will you…?*).

points.title: Predictions: I think it will…, probably
points.summary: Use **will** for predictions based on opinion or experience, often with *I think, I'm sure, probably, I expect*: *I think it'll be a great party.*

points.title: Shall: offers, suggestions and formal rules
points.summary: **Shall I / shall we** + base verb for offers and suggestions (mainly British). In formal documents, **shall** = must: *The tenant shall pay the rent monthly.*

points.title: Won't for refusals: The door won't open
points.summary: **won't** = refuses to (people) or doesn't work (things): *He **won't** listen to me. The car **won't** start.*

points.title: Will for habits and characteristic behaviour
points.summary: **will** can describe typical behaviour or habits (*She'll sit there for hours*) and, when stressed, annoying insistence (*He **will** leave his socks on the floor!*).

points.title: Decision now (will) or decided before (going to)?
points.summary: **will** = I decide at the moment of speaking. **going to** = I decided before: *We've run out of milk. ~ I'll buy some.* / *I'm going to buy milk later.*

points.title: Predictions: opinion (will) or evidence (going to)?
points.summary: **will** for predictions based on opinion, belief or experience: *I think you'll like it.* **going to** for predictions based on evidence now: *Look out! It's going to fall!*

points.title: Will, going to or present continuous?
points.summary: **present continuous** = fixed arrangements (*I'm meeting Ali at 6*). **going to** = intentions (*I'm going to learn Spanish*). **will** = decisions now, predictions, promises.

points.title: When both are possible, and formal uses of will
points.summary: Often **will** and **going to** are both correct, with a small difference: *going to* links the future to the present situation; *will* sounds more neutral, formal or certain.

points.title: Wish + past simple: things you want to be different now
points.summary: **wish + past simple** for a present situation you don't like: *I **wish** I **lived** near the sea.* (I don't.)

points.title: Wish + could: abilities and possibilities
points.summary: **wish + could** for something you can't do now: *I **wish** I **could** swim. I **wish** I **could** come to your party.*

points.title: Wish or hope?
points.summary: **hope** = something that is **possible**: *I hope you pass.* **wish** = something that **isn't** true or likely: *I wish I were younger.*

points.title: Wish + past perfect: regrets about the past
points.summary: **wish + past perfect** for something in the past you regret: *I **wish** I **hadn't eaten** so much.* (I ate too much.)

points.title: Wish + would: wanting someone or something to change
points.summary: **wish + would** to complain about someone's behaviour or a situation you want to change: *I **wish** you **would** stop interrupting!*

points.title: If only: a stronger wish
points.summary: **If only** = a stronger, more emotional *I wish*: *If only I had more time! If only I hadn't said that! If only he would call!*

points.title: Formal wish: I wish to…, wish for…
points.summary: In formal English, **wish + to-infinitive** = *want*: *I **wish to** complain.* **wish for** + noun = want something you don't have.

points.title: Subject + verb + object
points.summary: The normal order is **subject + verb + object** (*I like tea*). Don't put anything **between** the verb and its object: *I like tea very much* (not *I like very much tea*).

points.title: Place before time: at the station yesterday
points.summary: At the end of a sentence, put **place** before **time**: *I met her **at the station yesterday**.* With manner too, the usual order is **manner → place → time**: *She worked **hard at the office all day**.*

points.title: Where do adverbs go? Also, probably, already, only
points.summary: Many short adverbs go in the **middle** of the sentence: **before the main verb**, but **after** *be* and the first **auxiliary**: *I **also** like tea. She's **probably** at home. We've **already** eaten.*

points.title: Two objects: give me the book, give the book to me
points.summary: Verbs like ***give, send, show, lend, tell*** can have two objects: ***give** someone something* (*She gave me a present*) or ***give** something **to** someone* (*She gave a present to me*). With *buy, make, get, cook*, use ***for***.

points.title: Fronting for emphasis and here comes the bus
points.summary: For **emphasis** or **contrast**, English sometimes puts an object or phrase at the **start** (*That film I'll never forget*). After *here / there* and place phrases at the start, the verb can come **before** a noun subject (*Here comes the bus. On the hill stood an old castle.*).

would-be-get-used-to.h1: Be Used To and Get Used To

points.title: Used to do or be used to doing?
points.summary: **used to + base verb** = a past habit (not now). **be used to + -ing / noun** = it's familiar, normal for me.

points.title: Be used to: in all tenses
points.summary: **be used to** works in any tense: *I'm used to it. I wasn't used to it. I've never been used to it. You'll be used to it soon.*

points.title: Get used to: becoming familiar
points.summary: **get used to + -ing / noun** = the process of becoming familiar: *I'm getting used to my new job. It took me months to get used to the cold.*

points.title: Accustomed to, grow used to, and passive -ing after used to
points.summary: Formal alternatives: **be / become accustomed to + -ing / noun**. Gradual change: **grow used to**. Passive: **be used to being + past participle** (*I'm not used to being ignored*).

would-like.h1: Would Like, Would Rather and Prefer

points.title: I'd like…, Would you like…?
points.summary: **would like** + noun or **to + verb** = a polite *want*: *I'd like a tea. I'd like to go home.* **Would you like…?** offers and invites.

points.title: Like or would like?
points.summary: **like** = enjoy, in general: *I like swimming.* **would like** = want, now or on one occasion: *I'd like to swim now.*

points.title: I'd rather…: what you prefer
points.summary: **would rather + base verb** = would prefer: *I'd rather stay at home.* **would rather … than** compares two things: *I'd rather walk than take the bus.*

points.title: Prefer and would prefer
points.summary: **prefer** (in general): *I prefer tea **to** coffee. I prefer walking **to** driving.* **would prefer** (now): *I'd prefer **to** walk (**rather than** drive).*

points.title: I'd like you to…, I'd prefer you to…, I'd prefer it if…
points.summary: To talk about what you want **someone else** to do: **would like / would prefer + person + to + verb**, or **would prefer it if + past**: *I'd like you to call me.*

points.title: I would have liked to…, I'd rather have…
points.summary: For past wishes that didn't happen: **would have liked to + verb** (or *would like to have done*), **would rather have + past participle**, **would have preferred to**.

points.title: Zero conditional: always true
points.summary: **if / when + present simple, present simple** for facts and things that always happen: *If you mix red and white, you get pink.*

points.title: First conditional: a possible future
points.summary: **if + present simple, will + base verb** for a real possibility in the future: *If it rains, we'll stay at home.*

points.title: First conditional with can, might, should and imperatives
points.summary: The result can use other verbs: *If you're free, you **can** come. If it rains, we **might** stay in. If you see him, **tell** him.*

points.title: If or when?
points.summary: **when** = you're sure it will happen. **if** = it may or may not happen. *When I get home, I'll call you. If I get the job, I'll call you.*

points.title: Real conditionals with other tenses
points.summary: Real conditionals can use any tense that makes sense: *If you were at the meeting, you know the news. If she's arriving at 6, we should leave now.*

points.title: If you'll wait…: will and should in real if-clauses
points.summary: *Will* can go after *if* for **willingness**, **insistence** or a **later result**: *If you'll wait here, I'll get the manager.* *Should* after *if* = less likely.
